DATE
Friday, Nov. 6, 2026
CALL PARTICIPANTS
- Vice President of Investor Relations and Finance - Alan Peterson
- Chairman and Chief Executive Officer - Jeffrey Hanson
- President and Chief Operating Officer - Gabriel Willhite
- Chief Investment Officer - Stefan Oh
- Chief Financial Officer - Aric Chang
TAKEAWAYS
- Normalized FFO -- $0.58 per diluted share, representing 31.8% growth driven by accretive acquisitions and organic portfolio execution.
- Full Year 2026 NFFO Guidance -- $2.23 to $2.26 per diluted share, up from the previous range of $2.15 to $2.19, reflecting higher growth expectations across all property segments.
- Total Same-Store NOI Growth -- 13.8% year over year, marking the 11th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth for the portfolio.
- SHOP Same-Store NOI Growth -- 28.2% year over year, fueled by occupancy gains and a widening spread between revenue and expense growth.
- ISHC Same-Store NOI Growth -- 15.7% year over year, reflecting Trilogy's performance in occupancy and margin expansion.
- SHOP RevPOR Growth -- 5.4% year over year, driven by pricing power and a 34% reduction in rent concessions.
- SHOP ExPOR Growth -- 0.8% year over year, which propelled same-store NOI margin expansion of 350 basis points to 23.5%.
- Trilogy Same-Store Occupancy -- 91.2% on average, an increase of 110 basis points compared to the prior year.
- Trilogy Skilled Nursing Occupancy -- 90.2%, representing a sequential increase of 30 basis points despite typical seasonal lows for the segment.
- Trilogy Senior Housing Occupancy -- 92.6%, an increase of 70 basis points from the previous quarter.
- Total Completed Investments YTD -- 2.1 billion, consisting of 1.69 billion in third-quarter acquisitions across 17 communities.
- Investment Pipeline -- Over 1 billion in awarded deals, which management expects to close through the first quarter of 2027.
- Kensington Portfolio Acquisition -- $572 million for six communities, part of a larger eight-community agreement valued at approximately $873 million.
- LCB Senior Living Acquisition -- $696 million for eight communities, establishing a new operating footprint in the Northeast with 2020 to 2022 vintage assets.
- SHOP Portfolio Average Age -- 18.1 years, a decrease from 22.9 years at the end of 2025 following recent capital allocation toward newer properties.
- Net Debt to Annualized Adjusted EBITDA -- 1.9x, a 0.5-turn improvement sequentially driven by efficient balance sheet management and equity settlements.
- Total Liquidity -- Approximately 2.35 billion, including 1.32 billion in gross proceeds available from unsettled forward sale agreements.
- Trilogy Quality Mix -- 75.7% of resident days, an 80-basis-point increase year over year driven by preference from health systems and payers.
- Outpatient Medical Same-Store NOI Guidance -- 0.5% to 1.0%, representing a 25-basis-point increase to the range.
- Triple-Net Leased Same-Store NOI Guidance -- 2.5% to 3.5%, a 50-basis-point increase reflecting improved performance from underlying tenants.
Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]
RISKS
- Willhite warned that operating partners risk deteriorating their culture and performance by taking on too much growth too quickly, noting that the company is methodical about operator bench capacity.
SUMMARY
American Healthcare REIT, Inc. (AHR +3.34%) reported a transition into what management termed Phase 2 of its public lifespan, emphasizing platform enhancements and data-driven operational support for its regional partners. The company completed 2.1 billion in investments year to date, specifically targeting newer vintage senior housing assets in infill markets with high barriers to entry. Management increased its full-year 2026 earnings guidance based on sequential occupancy gains and expanded operating margins within its primary senior housing segments. The company also improved its leverage profile, reporting a net debt to annualized adjusted EBITDA ratio of 1.9x as it settled 1.88 billion in forward equity agreements during the quarter.
- Management reported that 2026 marks a phase focused on leaning into platform enhancements, expanding operator relationships, and supercharging data capabilities: President Willhite stated, "Phase 2 has been about leaning into platform enhancements, taking the company to a new level and making sure the company is built for the sustained growth."
- Management described certain acquisitions as occurring in "fortress markets" where development timelines can span five to nine years due to land scarcity: Chief Executive Officer Hanson stated, "we're allocating capital towards newer vintage senior housing in affluent, supply-constrained infill markets."
- The company is leveraging a revenue management playbook developed at Trilogy across its broader SHOP portfolio: President Willhite noted, "We've talked a lot about leveraging the Trilogy platform, their revenue management strategies and their revenue management playbook and rolling that out through our roster of operators."
- The company completed a 696 million acquisition that introduced LCB Senior Living to the platform, providing an immediate footprint in the Northeast: Chief Investment Officer Oh noted, "this series of transactions gives us our first meaningful footprint in the Northeast and establishes a long-sought relationship with LCB at immediate scale."
- Trilogy maintains a development pipeline of three to five new campuses annually, utilizing value-engineered prototypes to maintain returns: President Willhite indicated, "Trilogy has built over 80 properties themselves, developed themselves, and they value engineered the prototype."
- The company reported a 34% reduction in rent concessions year over year due to increased occupancy and pricing power: President Willhite stated, "we actually took our rent concession number down 34% year-over-year because of a hyper focus on that."
INDUSTRY GLOSSARY
- ExPOR: Expense per occupied room, a metric used to track the operating costs associated with filled units.
- ISHC: Integrated Senior Health Campuses, a segment that includes independent living, assisted living, memory care, and skilled nursing services under one campus.
- NFFO: Normalized Funds From Operations, a non-GAAP performance measure that adjusts NAREIT FFO for certain non-cash or non-recurring items.
- RevPOR: Revenue per occupied room, a key indicator of pricing power and resident rate levels.
- RIDEA: REIT Investment Diversification and Empowerment Act, a structure that allows REITs to participate in the operating income of healthcare properties.
- SHOP: Senior Housing Operating Properties, a segment where the REIT participates in the daily operations and financial results of the facilities.
- Trilogy: Trilogy Investors, LLC, a consolidated subsidiary of AHR that operates integrated senior health campuses.
Full Conference Call Transcript
Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the American Healthcare REIT Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Alan Peterson, Vice President of Investor Relations and Finance. Alan, please go ahead.
Alan Peterson: Good morning. Thank you for joining us for American Healthcare REIT's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. With me today are Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Jeff Hanson; President and Chief Operating Officer, Gabe Willhite; Chief Investment Officer, Stefan Oh; and Chief Financial Officer, Aric Chang. On today's call, Jeff, Gabe, Stefan and Aric will provide high-level commentary discussing our operational results, financial position, our increased 2026 guidance and other recent news relating to American Healthcare REIT. Following these remarks, we will conduct a question-and-answer session. Please be advised that this call will include forward-looking statements.
All statements made during this call other than statements of historical fact are forward-looking statements that are subject to numerous risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those projected in these statements. Therefore, you should exercise caution in interpreting and relying on them. I refer you to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of the risks that could impact our future operating results, financial condition and prospects. All forward-looking statements speak only as of today, November 6, 2026, or such other date as may otherwise be specified.
We assume no obligation to update or revise any forward-looking statements, whether as a result of new information, future events or otherwise, except as required by law. During the call, we will discuss certain non-GAAP financial measures, which we believe can be useful in evaluating the company's operating performance. These measures should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for our financial results prepared in accordance with GAAP. Reconciliations of non-GAAP financial measures discussed on this call to the most directly comparable measures calculated in accordance with GAAP are included in our earnings release, supplemental information package and our filings with the SEC.
You can find these documents as well as an audio webcast replay of this conference call on the Investor Relations section of our website at www.americanhealthcarereit.com. With that, I'll turn the call over to AHR's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Jeff Hanson.
Jeffrey Hanson: Thanks, Alan, and good morning, everyone. Last quarter, I discussed the durability of AHR's competitive advantages and our progress in scaling this company with both ambition and discipline to drive compounding earnings growth for shareholders. This quarter, I'd like to advance that story one step further. First, the headline results for the quarter. Total same-store NOI growth of 13.8%, our 11th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth with both our SHOP and ISHC or Trilogy segments benefiting from increasing operating spreads and significant margin expansion as well. Another increase in full year guidance, which now implies at the midpoint, full year NFFO per diluted share growth of over 30% versus last year.
Strong external growth with $2.1 billion in completed investments year-to-date and an awarded pipeline of more than $1 billion, a significant portion of which was secured on relationship, not price. None of that pipeline is reflected in our revised guidance, and all of it is expected to be match funded with proceeds from our unsettled forward sale agreements. And lastly, efficient balance sheet management as we continue to materially deleverage while generating significant growth, which is highlighted by net debt to EBITDA of just 1.9x at quarter end. These figures matter individually, but what matters more is what they say collectively. Our strategy is working, and it's fueling our ability to build on our track record for continued growth.
AHR has multiple engines of value creation working simultaneously. organic operating growth, accretive external investment, internally generated development and an increasingly sophisticated operating platform. And we've accelerated growth and upgraded portfolio quality while simultaneously strengthening the balance sheet, which is positioning us with real capacity to keep playing offense going forward. Put simply, this is not just a larger AHR, it's a more capable AHR, one in which our platform's core competencies are increasingly working together as an integrated system to produce consistently strong results that are beginning to compound. The sector tailwind is not the AHR advantage as we often say internally. Our platform and our execution is.
The team will run through the operating details in a moment, but the progression you'll hear is important. These results are proof points that our operating model is creating tangible value. We believe high-quality real estate is imperative, but not sufficient to produce the best results. Superior results are achieved by partnering with the strongest operators and enhancing their ability to execute. As an operating REIT, we increasingly think about AHR as a dynamic operating platform. The model combines institutional scale, resources and capital with proven regional operating expertise and then surrounds those operators with resources that can make already strong businesses even better. That's where durable value is created. And it all starts in our communities.
The quality of care and outcomes our operating partners deliver every day is the foundation of everything that we do. Strong clinical outcomes earn trust and trust is ultimately what drives occupancy, rate and payer mix. In our business has done well, quality of care and financial performance move together. Turning to external growth. The headline is more opportunity, same standard. Our external growth activity remains significant, but the emphasis must remain where it belongs. Long-term per share value creation is the objective, and that's the driving force behind everything that we've done this year. Importantly, external growth is not simply adding NOI. It's reshaping the quality and risk profile of the enterprise.
We're allocating capital towards newer vintage senior housing in affluent, supply-constrained infill markets where operating growth and pricing power is embedded in real estate that's very difficult to replicate, which is a powerful combination. Our $3 billion plus of closed and pipeline investments represent assets that are all accretive to first year NFFO, accretive to NAV per share, enhance overall portfolio quality and are expected to be meaningful contributors to both NFFO per share growth and same-store NOI growth for years to come. Importantly, these $3 billion in investments reflect an average vintage of 2019, representing some of the highest quality senior housing product in some of the best markets in the country.
On our August call, I described our approach to today's sector opportunity as measured aggression. We'll continue to move decisively when quality, basis, operator, market and expected returns meet our standard. That combination, speed and execution when opportunity meets preparedness and patience when it does not is what we mean by the measured aggression reference. And given our reputation, our relationships and our track record, much of what we pursue never reaches the broader market. We're taking the same approach to scaling the platform. We've been deliberately investing in conjunction with and ahead of robust growth. Over the last several months, we've strengthened critical leadership capabilities across our finance, investments, strategic asset management and enterprise technology divisions.
These hires introduce added depth to an already strong team, and they're the architecture for the company we're scaling AHR into. Gabe will cover these details in a moment. I also want to recognize Brian Peay, who retired on September 30 after a decade of service. He helped guide AHR through a period of remarkable growth and our listing on the New York Stock Exchange, and he leaves us with a strong financial foundation. We're grateful for his leadership and for his support of a smooth transition, and we certainly wish him well in retirement. We're also pleased to welcome Aric Chang, who joined us on October 1.
Aric comes to AHR from Public Storage, an S&P 500 operating intensive REIT, where revenue management, data and capital deployment drive results. The same discipline is at the center of AHR's operating business. His experience brings together a rare combination of what the next phase of AHR requires. We welcome Aric, and you'll hear from him later in the call. I'd like to close with a central point. The demographic opportunity in the sector is certainly extraordinary, but it will not determine the winners. Expertise and execution will. We believe AHR is increasingly positioned at the intersection of historically strong sector fundamentals and an integrated operating and capital allocation platform built to convert those fundamentals into superior long-term shareholder value.
We remain early in this opportunity, and we're intensely focused on ensuring that the best version of AHR is still ahead of us. With that, I'll turn the call over to Gabe, who will walk you through the operating results and other important details from the quarter.
Gabriel Willhite: Thanks, Jeff. 2026 marks a new phase for AHR. While Phase 1 was about entering the public market and proving what we knew we could do as a company, Phase 2 has been about leaning into platform enhancements, taking the company to a new level and making sure the company is built for the sustained growth and value creation opportunities that we see today. We've expanded our operator relationships. We've enhanced our asset management and operator support functionality, and we're supercharging our data capabilities. I'm happy to report it's working. Total portfolio same-store NOI grew 13.8% year-over-year, accelerating from 13.2% in the second quarter, which was already a high watermark.
Together, Trilogy and SHOP make our SHOP+ portfolio and both segments took occupancy higher and at the same time, expanded margin again. The setup we described to you in August is now in the results, and we feel confident about the future. Stepping back, our portfolio and strategy rests on 2 core beliefs. First, that the resiliency that comes from the more needs-based portion of the broader senior housing continuum will drive relative outperformance. Second, that there's absolutely no substitute for elite operating partners. There's no better example of those beliefs than Trilogy. And once again, Trilogy delivered another impressive quarter, growing same-store NOI 15.7% year-over-year and 1.6% sequentially.
Same-store occupancy averaged 91.2%, roughly 110 basis points ahead of a year ago. Now you'll recall in August, we characterized the second quarter skilled nursing occupancy step down in seasonality. And while the third quarter is typically a seasonal low for skilled nursing, Trilogy skilled nursing occupancy actually overcame that seasonality and further increased to 90.2%, up 30 basis points sequentially. Senior housing occupancy also grew across campuses, reaching 92.6%, up 70 basis points sequentially. Trilogy also delivered on expense controls, further bolstering margin. Same-store revenue grew 4.8%, while same-store operating expenses grew 2.2% with controllable costs actually down 3.7% year-over-year. And same-store NOI margin finished 21%, roughly 200 basis points ahead of last year.
As those more familiar with Trilogy know, there's many levers that drive growth. Quality mix in Trilogy's post-acute care business is an important one. Quality mix reached 75.7% of same-store resident days, up roughly 80 basis points from a year ago. The continued improvement you're seeing in quality mix is a result of being the preferred option as health systems, physicians and Medicare Advantage plans alike look to high-quality care providers, and that's important.
Trilogy's focus on care also shows up in its overall CMS star ratings across the portfolio, which are now sitting at 4.2 stars and its quality measure ratings, which are now sitting at 4.8 stars on average, both industry-leading among the largest skilled nursing operators in the country. Turning to SHOP. This quarter by every measure was a standout. Same-store NOI grew 28.2% year-over-year, accelerating from 20.5% in the second quarter and growing 9.1% sequentially. Same-store occupancy averaged 90%. Same-store revenue grew 9%, driven by accelerating RevPOR growth of 5.4% year-over-year. And notably, ExPOR grew just 0.8%. So the RevPOR to ExPOR spread expanded to roughly 460 basis points.
That widening spread unlocks tremendous value and propelled same-store NOI margin expansion of 350 basis points year-over-year to 23.5% and ultimately, strong NOI growth. When we say that execution matters, this is what we're talking about. Demographics alone do not do that work for us. All of the work that we continue to do to ensure our operators have the full strength and backing of our platform is having an effect as we evaluate the results we've achieved. And that work isn't done, and it probably never will be. And we will continue to evaluate opportunities to further enhance our operating capabilities across our portfolio through data and analytics, the Trilogy platform, our innovation forums and our strategic asset management.
It's important to note the scale of our SHOP segment has grown materially. SHOP now spans 109 properties and over 10,000 units, up from 71 properties and over 5,700 units a year ago. We're excited to have these assets on our platform and I have no doubt that our strategy of pairing the highest quality assets with the highest quality operators will allow us to continue to build upon the results we've already achieved. And in furtherance of that mission, I'm excited to expand on some of our talent acquisition.
Ann Lacey joined us in September as Executive Vice President, Portfolio and Asset Management for Senior Housing, and her mandate is to drive our multimodal operator support system across our growing portfolio. Ann is a highly capable expert who will draw from a rare and sought-after background. She spent 7 years at one of the best private equity investors in the senior housing space and prior to that, spent over 11 years with Sunrise Senior Living, a leading senior housing operator.
Jon Crosier, our new Chief Technology Officer, is leading the data and technology strategy that, among other things, puts the revenue management, analytics and reporting tools we built alongside Trilogy in the hands of more of our regional operating partners every quarter. Jon will draw on experience in both the public and the private sector, having worked at the Irvine Company, one of the most sophisticated private real estate companies in the U.S. And also just this week, we added the Jon's team from the health care REIT industry, further enhancing our capabilities. Together, Ann and Jon will help drive performance across the portfolio and operators, unlocking innovation through collaboration in an industry that rewards you for doing so.
They are already making an impact and are poised to help us further enhance the platform for multiyear growth. I want to close by extending my gratitude to our regional operating partners and our asset management team. They produce this quarter in our communities one resident at a time. And I know they all agree that care will always come first. And when you operate with that conviction, the results will follow. With that, I'll turn it over to Stefan.
Stefan K. Oh: Thanks, Gabe. The third quarter was transformative for our SHOP portfolio. We meaningfully enhanced the quality of the portfolio through our recent acquisitions. Not only are the assets exceptional in many ways, but the operators we partner with are equally impressive. How we acquired these properties was also important. As Jeff and Gabe alluded to earlier, every deal is won on partnership, but not always on price, and that proved to be valuable this quarter. During the third quarter, we closed approximately $1.69 billion of new investments across 17 senior housing communities. That brings us to the $2.1 billion of completed investments year-to-date that Jeff referenced. Two transactions in particular defined the quarter.
The first was our acquisition of properties owned and operated by Kensington Senior Living. To date, we have closed on 6 Class A communities for approximately $572 million. These are part of an 8-community portfolio carrying an aggregate contract purchase price of approximately $873 million. What made this portfolio so compelling starts with the real estate. Kensington purpose-built 7 of the 8 communities, approximately 93% of the units are dedicated to assisted living and memory care, and the communities sit in affluent infill submarkets across the Los Angeles, San Francisco Bay Area, Washington, D.C. and New York metropolitan areas, where developable land is scarce, zoning is restrictive and entitlement time lines are prolonged.
The opportunity reached us through a limited channel process rather than a broadly marketed auction, and we were not the highest bidder. Kensington as both owner and operator selected AHR based on alignment and long-term partnership. The transaction formally establishes our relationship with Kensington, and we expect to close on the remaining 2 communities by year-end. The second introduced LCB Senior Living to the AHR platform as a key operator in the Northeast. In that series of transactions, we acquired 8 communities for approximately $696 million across East Coast markets, all built between 2020 and 2022.
7 of those are now managed by LCB and with 5 of the communities developed by them, they bring development capabilities in the same way Kensington does. In all, 10 communities were marketed together and only a solution for all 10 was going to clear the market. Rather than walk away from a highly strategic opportunity or stretch our capital allocation discipline to take all 10, we secured all of the assets and assigned the 2 communities that did not fit our strategy to another investor at our allocated basis. This series of transactions gives us our first meaningful footprint in the Northeast and establishes a long-sought relationship with LCB at immediate scale.
Beyond those 2 deals, we have closed $800 million of investments this year that have been a continuation of our strategy to expand with many of our existing regional operating partners in the markets where they already excel. This results in an average deal size of approximately $114 million and is comprised of single asset transactions and smaller portfolios. This is how we derisk external growth while adding market share in the regions we have identified as offering among the best risk-adjusted returns. Ultimately, what matters most is how these investments are enhancing our portfolio.
We have been deliberately allocating capital towards newer vintage senior housing in affluent supply-constrained markets and the average age of the SHOP portfolio now stands at 18.1 years compared with 22.9 at the end of 2025. The result is a newer, higher-quality portfolio with an increasingly attractive long-term risk-adjusted return profile. In addition, our relative scale provides an advantage. We don't face the pacing pressures for external growth that we would if we were larger, while also allowing us to significantly enhance the overall portfolio quality relatively quickly. Looking ahead, our awarded pipeline stands at over $1 billion, which includes newly awarded deals as well as those previously disclosed.
We expect a portion of those to close late in the fourth quarter and the remainder to close during the first quarter of 2027. In addition, we continue to see a robust acquisition market with ample opportunity to strategically grow with our operators through single asset or small portfolio transactions. And as our expanding network of operators takes us into new regions of the country, the available opportunities also continue to expand, allowing us to maintain our focus and discipline on growth. Finally, I want to reiterate the importance we place on choosing our operating partners.
Their commitment to the highest standards of care and resident experience is what ultimately allows our communities to perform at their highest levels and remain competitive over the long term. Those standards are nonnegotiable for AHR. And as demonstrated by the Kensington transaction, this isn't a one-sided process. The alignment has to be felt by both sides to truly create the partnership and trust that allows us to be their capital partner of choice and for them to be our preferred operating partner. When we pair the strength of our operators with our disciplined acquisition strategy and underwriting standards, we believe the outcome is a better resident experience and strong investment performance. With that, I'll turn it over to Aric.
Aric Chang: Thanks, Stefan, and thank you, Jeff, for the kind words. Before I get into the numbers, a brief word. For months before I joined, I watched this team execute on the plan AHR committed to. Now several weeks from the inside, I can say with confidence that AHR is exactly the top-tier organization that it looked like from the outside. I'm proud to be part of this team and to be delivering our 3Q results. I'll cover 3 items: third quarter financial performance, our updated full year guidance and our balance sheet and liquidity profile. We reported normalized FFO of $0.58 per diluted share for the third quarter, up 31.8% from the same quarter last year.
This was driven by strong execution from our operating partners and asset management teams alongside our investment teams, delivering accretive acquisitions to our growing portfolio. Given these results, we are now raising full year 2026 NFFO per diluted share guidance to a range of $2.23 to $2.26, up from our prior range of $2.15 to $2.19. At the midpoint, that represents over 30% NFFO per diluted share growth over 2025. We're also raising total portfolio same-store NOI growth guidance to a range of 12% to 14%. At the midpoint of guidance, that is up 100 basis points versus the previous guidance midpoint, and it's driven by higher growth expectations across all of our property segments.
At the segment level, Trilogy same-store NOI growth moves to a range of 14.5% to 16.5%, up 100 basis points. SHOP moves to a range of 23% to 26%, up 500 basis points. Outpatient medical moves to a range of 0.5% to 1%, up 25 basis points and triple-net properties moved to a range of 2.5% to 3.5%, up 50 basis points. As always, this guidance reflects only the transactions and capital markets activity completed through today and no additional acquisitions beyond what is closed year-to-date. Guidance does not include any of the awarded deals still in the pipeline. While we're raising our outlook for same-store NOI and earnings, our G&A guidance is unchanged.
We're strengthening the platform with talent and scaling efficiently, which means more of our growth is reaching the bottom line. Now turning to the balance sheet. Net debt to annualized adjusted EBITDA improved to 1.9x, 0.5 turn lower sequentially and 1.6 turns lower than a year ago. On liquidity, we remain well funded to support our growth. As of today, we have approximately $1.3 billion of gross proceeds available under unsettled forward sales agreements relating to 24.6 million shares, along with full $850 million of capacity under our lines of credit. The takeaway is simple. We are already fully funded for our awarded pipeline of over $1 billion plus additional future investment opportunities.
Having worked at some of the industry's best capitalized REITs, I'm pleased to say that my philosophy on capital allocation and capital structure aligns closely with the strategy AHR has already employed to date. My focus is now twofold: sharpening and expanding the capital tools already at our disposal and effectively communicating our strategy to the market. You should expect enhanced disclosure and greater visibility around how we intend to fund growth and manage our capital structure over the long term. We'll continue to be strategic about when and how we raise capital, only doing so when we can deploy it accretively to grow both long-term earnings and NAV.
On a personal note, I've enjoyed getting to know many of our analysts, investors and operating partners in my short time here, and I look forward to continuing those conversations. I'd like to close by thanking the entire AHR team for their warm welcome and for what they've accomplished so far this year, strong operating results, record investment activity while materially reducing leverage, putting us on track for full year 2026 NFFO per diluted share growth of over 30%. Those accomplishments are a reflection of the 2 things Jeff opened with, ambition and discipline.
We're upgrading and strengthening our portfolio, team and balance sheet all at the same time without losing sight of our core mission to deliver high-quality care and outcomes for our residents. That's the philosophy that enables AHR to continue creating long-term durable value for our shareholders. And with that, operator, we'd like to open the line for questions.
Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question is from Farrell Granath with Bank of America.
Farrell Granath: Welcome, Aric, your first earnings call with us at AHR. So I first wanted to touch on your acquisition pipeline. I appreciate all the details, especially for what you've been acquiring. But now just looking forward, you've refueled your pipeline. I'm hoping you can give a little bit more color on the type of momentum really that you're seeing and the quality of product that you're seeing come into the market, especially as it seems that you're targeting that newer vintage type of asset.
Stefan K. Oh: Farrell, this is Stefan. I appreciate the question. I'd say, first of all, obviously, what we've been acquiring, we're really excited about the portfolio that we're building. And quite frankly, we are not seeing anything that's indicating that the deal volume in the market is slowing down. It's continuing to be very good. It's a strong deal flow. We are continuing to underwrite deals that are working for both us and our operating partners. And we're going to continue to be looking at very high-quality newer assets. A good majority of it is going to be in infill markets, high barrier-to-entry markets. But we're also going to be continuing to look at those strong secondary markets as well.
If you look at the pipeline that we have right now, most of those assets are actually in the same MSAs as the headquarters of our operators. And we're continuing to grow with our existing operators. We're continuing to stick with our strategy. I mean it has been working really well. And I think the way we have handled our growth and our partnership with our operators continues to pay off. They are bringing us a lot of off-market deals. We're getting a lot of deals through relationships. So we can be selective as we continue to grow. But I think there are going to continue to be a lot of opportunities for us to look at and bid on.
Farrell Granath: Great. And I guess also on that point, especially when it comes to the scaling of your SHOP portfolio, I know that you've been able to expand not only in geographic, but also in your partnership with different operators. A little bit on the lessons learned or as you're scaling, what are items that you're very focused on as you continue with this momentum in your pipeline?
Jeffrey Hanson: Yes. Farrell, Jeff Hanson. Good question. Thank you for that. Look, I think the strategy that is actually differentiated and fairly unique to AHR in terms of how we grow externally, it's really a two-pronged approach that we've been communicating the same way since the earliest roadshows for the IPO. We're either expanding with existing trusted operators that are already in our stable in market areas that they already compete very effectively with that materially derisk the external growth proposition. And when we do go into new regions with new operating partners, it's highly circumspect, very strategic, and it's usually going to be with size and scale.
This year, 2026 is a perfect example of that two-pronged strategy, LCB portfolio and the Kensington portfolio being perfect examples of the latter, while we're simultaneously executing over $800 million in deals that represent expansions with existing trusted operators. So again, that kind of expansion, especially with the -- Stefan didn't mention this, but a lot of what we brought from our operators happen to be already managed by our operators for other capital that's ready to exit. That's the quintessential derisking of external growth. And the last thing that I would point out there is we've grown from 8 to 11 SHOP operators outside of Trilogy this year.
If we were okay with expanding our operator base in a year to 2 dozen, we literally could have done another $2 billion plus in deals this year that would have met our requirements in terms of asset and location quality, but that's not our playbook. That's not our strategy. And we think that very intentional strategic and aggressive growth with existing operators and our stable, not only derisks but drives greater results in the long term and certainly a better risk-adjusted return profile overall.
Gabriel Willhite: And Farrell, it's Gabe. I'd just add an important nuance to that. We don't view operators as commodities that can be traded. We view them as long-term partnerships and it really having an impact on our performance to be partnered with an all-star team of operators. So we'll be more selective as we scale, and we actually find the operators before we find the investment opportunities as we start to scale. And then we look back on 10 and 15 years of doing senior housing, investing through the RIDEA structure and what are the lessons learned from that as we scale as well.
One of the big takeaways, and this is an important thing because I think new entrants probably can't draw from that experience is how even good operators can get over their skis and it can impact our total performance. And one of the ways that we've seen that happen over and over again is just taking on too much too fast and getting spread too thin and deteriorating the culture and the -- ultimately, the performance. So when we're looking to scale, Stefan and his team are looking for multiple outlets to grow with so that we are not overwhelming the operator bench that we have. We're very methodical about it.
And we want to make sure that our growth ambitions are aligned with the capabilities and the capacity of our operator bench. So that's a critical part of the whole proposition.
Jeffrey Hanson: And Stefan alluded to it briefly in his prepared remarks, our relative size advantage, and I think this is important. It means that we don't have to capture the entire market. to generate meaningful and attractive external growth for our shareholders. We simply need to capture the right opportunities at the right basis and with the right operating partners, which is exactly what we've done all year long. No shortage of opportunities. This year's volume industry-wide has been 2x what last year's was. And the vast majority of the capital markets teams on the brokerage side that control 80% or 90% of the SHOP product are all saying generally the same thing.
They're expecting the same level of velocity next year.
Operator: Your next question is from Ronald Kamdem with Morgan Stanley.
Ronald Kamdem: Great. Starting with the SHOP portfolio, the same-store guide raise of 500 basis points. I guess I was hoping we could double-click into that between pricing, occupancy and expense controls, maybe give us a sense of like what really outperformed your expectations? And obviously, as we flip the calendar to next year, just some thoughts on the durability of that outperformance.
Gabriel Willhite: Thanks, Ron. It's Gabe. So a few things go into that, and there's always multiple levers in this business. It's an operating business. You need to approach it as such. So what we were really happy to see this quarter over the last one is great sequential occupancy growth at the same time, pricing power within the portfolio driving RevPOR from 3.8% at the beginning of the year to 5.4% today. And I think it's important to note, by the way, our same-store universe doesn't change as the year goes on. We said it at the beginning of the year.
So this is an apples-to-apples comparison of what's going on and illustrates the value of having great operators, but also having a platform layered on top of that, that can help those operators achieve even more success than they would if they weren't on AHR's platform. We've talked a lot about leveraging the Trilogy platform, their revenue management strategies and their revenue management playbook and rolling that out through our roster of operators. It is having an impact, and that is one of the ways that we're able to grow RevPOR at that level. Those advantages are structural and embedded in our portfolio.
So we feel like we're poised well to take advantage of the really generational opportunity in senior housing today. So we feel good about 2027 and our ability to outperform expectations as we move through the opportunity ahead of us.
Aric Chang: Ron, it's Aric. Nice to chat with you again. One thing I'll add is while we won't get too in the weeds on '27, you asked about durability. If you look at what's implied for Q4 with our revised guidance, it's basically a repeat of a really outstanding high 20% print in Q3. So that should give you some signs that we feel really confident in the durability.
Ronald Kamdem: Great. Really helpful. And then my second question is just on the Trilogy side of it. I just would love to hear as you transition from sort of occupancy gains to pricing gains and incremental margins, just how that business has been evolving at this stage?
Gabriel Willhite: Ron, it's Gabe again. It kind of varies. It's dynamic, right? And Trilogy's business has a lot of levers to pull to drive the NOI performance. We have with Trilogy, not only one of the best operators in the space, but we also have a management contract that we think is the most aligned in the space as well to the bottom line. So Trilogy, better than probably anybody else is focused on every incremental way that they can grow that NOI.
So right now, what's going on with their business is, for the first time, maybe this summer selling season on the private pay side, less focus on running promotions and more focused on capturing residents at the right rate and building occupancy at the right rate. We saw that work very well in an even higher and higher occupancy environment. As we all know, rate management and revenue management is going to become a more critical part of the business. On the post-acute care side of their business, it's all about mix shift still today and tapping into the opportunities that come from being more highly occupied.
As you know, from knowing Trilogy well, Medicare and Medicare Advantage are the preferred reimbursement sources for the residents that are moving in there. And even within Medicare Advantage, there are literally hundreds of Medicare Advantage plans that Trilogy works to optimize and prioritize the partners that are willing to pay them for the quality of care that they provide because that comes at a higher cost than the low-quality providers. And they're always looking for partners who are willing to meet the reimbursement level for the high quality of care.
So as they optimize that, I think you'll continue to see good rate growth out of Trilogy, probably on the Medicare Advantage side, significantly above the Medicare rate increases as we've seen over the last 11 quarters.
Operator: Your next question is from Michael Goldsmith with UBS.
Michael Goldsmith: Maybe continuing the same line, your occupancy has now hit 90%. We've heard from others, right? And when you hit that 90% level of occupancy, the algorithm shifts from occupancy to rate. So I just wanted to get your perspective on that and then just talk a little bit about how you've been positioning yourself as you -- for when you reach this point when you can start to continue to maybe push rate a little bit harder.
Gabriel Willhite: Thanks for the question, Michael. This is not a new dynamic for us. We are -- 2 years ago, we started seeing higher occupied buildings more relying on revenue management. than on occupancy gains in order to drive NOI. So 2 years ago was when we partnered with Trilogy to bring in a revenue management expert that came from aviation and hospitality background, highly dynamic pricing models to help come up with strategies at Trilogy that can optimize revenue management there. That has been working for a long time at -- within Trilogy's portfolio, which, as you know, is over 50% of our NOI.
That -- we're tapping into that playbook and those strategies and have been for the better -- for over a year now with our other operators to focus there. That is where the future is in this business for NOI growth, certainly. There's still, though, let's not forget, at 90%, our goal is not to remain at 90% occupied in our portfolio. We're still working to grow occupancy, and we still have several years of occupancy gains that are going to fuel strong NOI growth. Just backing up because I think this is a question everybody wants to know, how sustainable is the NOI growth? And what level is it going to be and for how long?
So let's just talk about that for a second, right? Our strategy, our portfolio, our platform are working. 28% NOI growth on a same-store basis actually accelerated meaningfully from last quarter. And that's this year's NOI growth coming off of 2025 Q3's NOI growth, which was on a same-store basis over 25% as well. So we feel like we're going to be as well positioned as anybody to take advantage of the supply-demand dynamics in senior housing today and the runway that we have. So let's focus on what we actually do know and not speculate about where we go from here. We absolutely know that RevPOR growth is stronger as things get more highly occupied.
So we expect to see that. We absolutely know that we are at the very front end of an incredible demand surge with the baby boomer generation. That's going to put even more pressure on occupancies higher and create even more demand for the product. And we know that being more AL and memory care focused in the higher acuity side of the senior housing continuum, not only makes our portfolio more defensive, but it provides more runway for that demand. People won't be priced out by a discretionary decision about where to live. So if you would have asked us 2 years ago, what is the NOI growth going to be in your SHOP portfolio?
I don't think we would have said we're going to do 25% the first year, and then we're going to follow that up with 28% the year after, but we would have been right. So where do we go 2 years from now? I think we have the right platform, the right portfolio to drive outperformance. We've demonstrated that we can do it, and we feel well positioned to take advantage of a supply-demand dynamic that's only getting better from here.
Jeffrey Hanson: Yes. Gabe, that's excellent. And Michael, I'd add one thing. This is Jeff here. We're seeing this show up in our outperformance in terms of underwriting -- acquisition underwriting versus actual that we do every quarter. All of the $1 billion roughly that we bought in 2025 as of Q3 this year is materially outperforming underwriting and our underwriting actually hasn't changed. Double digit and the outperformance is roughly double -- low double digit in terms of NOI, which means initial first year cap rate to the upside of almost 75 basis points.
So not only are the operators that we're adding to the platform and expanding with performing exceedingly well, but the value that we're able to add after we absorb new assets is meaningful. So I think the main takeaway there is we're not just getting bigger. We're getting better as a platform.
Michael Goldsmith: Falls right into my follow-up question about the operating platform as a differentiator. To your point, you're outperforming your underwriting. What can you attribute that to specifically? Is it the revenue management side? Is it the analytics? Is it the asset management capabilities? Just trying to get what is the core tenet that's driving that outperformance of your underwriting?
Jeffrey Hanson: It's all of the above. It's broad-based. Gabe, do you want to elaborate?
Gabriel Willhite: Yes. What we -- first, what you need to do is start with great real estate, and you need to pair the great real estate with the highest quality operators in the country. You have those 2 things, you're ahead of pretty much everybody else, and you're going to get good results. But of course, being AHR, we're not satisfied with just those 2 things. So our strategy and our thinking is how do we take it further from here? How do we get better from here? How do we drive outperformance from here? And it becomes the operator support ecosystem.
So all credit to our investment team for doing $2.1 billion of assets that are 2019 vintage or newer this year, that creates the opportunity for the operators. But when we layer on data and analytics that helps with benchmarking and real-time performance visibility, portfolio-wide dashboards, pricing and CapEx intel with the Trilogy platform, which can help with revenue management, search engine optimization, employee experience, our innovation forums that bring this roster of best-in-class operators together to leverage more than just Trilogy's ideas because let me be clear, our other operators have great ideas and ideas can be leveraged throughout the platform as well. So creating a forum for them to be able to do that has been critically important.
And the final component of it is having a bench of asset managers with now Ann Lacey leading the charge that have real operational experience and have actually been in charge of making sure that the buildings are fully optimized. So they can come in as kind of a high-end consulting agency and take maybe underperforming assets or even the highest performing assets and make them better with our asset management team. All those things come together, and that's what creates the value, and that's what leads to outperform.
Operator: Your next question is from Michael Carroll with RBC Capital Markets.
Michael Carroll: I wanted to dig into Trilogy's results a little bit more. I know that, Gabe, you mentioned that they have some expense saving initiatives in place and the controllable expenses actually declined year-over-year. Can you give us a little bit of details on why the controllable expenses declined? What did they do? And is this just kind of a onetime decline? Or is this going to be ongoing over the next several quarters? Yes. So...
Gabriel Willhite: Trilogy does a lot of things well. All credit to them. If the Trilogy team is listening to this call, thank you, guys. We appreciate you, and we -- and I know you know that already, but I want the world to know it as well. So it's not -- for them, it's everything. They look at everything all the time. They're constantly looking at how they can run their business more efficiently. This quarter, it just happened to be looking at employee benefits and getting some cost savings around employee benefits without eroding the quality of those benefits is what they were able to capture.
So it is more of a onetime thing, Mike, but also at the same time, it's not -- it's repeatable because it's Trilogy being Trilogy, just finding ways to optimize the business, expand the margin and grow NOI and the best alignment in the industry.
Michael Carroll: Okay. Great. And then just looking at like the broader portfolio, I know we spent a lot of time talking about SHOP and the Trilogy portfolio. What about the other assets? I mean, is there an opportunity to maybe sell some noncore assets? Is that something that the company is looking at a little bit more in focus as you're being -- growing much more significantly in other parts of the portfolio?
Jeffrey Hanson: Sure. Yes, Jeff here. Thanks, Mike. Yes, we always do, as you know. First of all, our RIDEA vertical, both SHOP and Trilogy is the go-forward engine for AHR. So our capital, our platform expansion efforts and our external growth is exclusively focused there. I think what you're asking is as it relates to the OM portfolio, and I'll say what I think I said in the Q&A last quarter, we understand the value that's embedded in that portfolio. We've already sold 1/3 of the assets. We've taken NOI contribution from 35% down to roughly 10%, and that continues to drop rapidly. That's by design. And we've been net sellers will continue to be.
We're always looking for ways to drive long-term shareholder value and seeking optionality in doing so.
Operator: Your next question is from Wes Golladay with Baird.
Wesley Golladay: Maybe just sticking with the topic of dispositions. There is a strong transaction market for senior housing. Do you have any interest over the next year or so selling into that, maybe some of your older assets that no longer fit the go-forward criteria?
Gabriel Willhite: Yes. Thanks, Wes. We're constantly looking at the portfolio and evaluating disposition candidates. Sometimes it's because they're older and noncore. Sometimes it's because we feel like we've gotten all the value out of it that we can, and we've taken it to the highest level, and that might be a market-driven decision. At the end of the day, it might be you're looking at your micro markets and where new supply is coming. So tracking that is pretty critical to seeing where you might have vulnerability. So we are doing that. We -- and it's something we'll continue to do. Nothing to announce just yet on what types of dispositions you might expect for 2027.
But I'd expect early in 2027, we may have more to report there.
Wesley Golladay: Okay. And then with the election results earlier in the week, did anything stand out to you, either positive or negative at the local level?
Gabriel Willhite: At the national level, I think it's most relevant to Trilogy's business. And having a split Congress and White House means that the base case for us is that there's not going to be a lot of change in the skilled nursing industry, both from a regulation perspective and a reimbursement perspective. So I think it's business as usual there and predictability in an environment where Trilogy has been able to drive outperformance seems to be a favorable outcome. At the local level, nothing to really highlight just yet. We'll see how things play out.
Of course, we are always tracking what states we're in and what's happening in those states to make sure that we're regarding our risks from regulation as well. And I think at this point, nothing meaningful that's going to change our strategy.
Operator: Your next question is from Austin Wurschmidt with KeyBanc Capital Markets.
Austin Wurschmidt: Just going back to Trilogy for a minute, recognizing NOI growth hasn't slowed. You have seen revenue growth slow a little bit for maybe some of the reasons you highlighted on the call of occupancy being a little bit higher, even though that does continue to ratchet up. But can the Med Advantage opportunity and just Q mix shifts that you've talked about as well as the opportunity set on the private pay senior housing side of the business, can those increases continue to drive or drive re-acceleration in the top line over time?
Gabriel Willhite: Yes. And I think a part of that, Austin, is Trilogy's unique business, having this integrated campus model. So for those unfamiliar, Trilogy has got post-acute care and private pay senior housing under one roof. And those 2 businesses have almost opposite inflection points on seasonality, where the senior housing part of the business from an occupancy perspective is strongest at the end of the summer and in the early fall. At the same time, the skilled nursing occupancy tends to be the weakest, and they are at vastly different revenue numbers, right?
So the post-acute care business might be 2x or 3x what the Trilogy private pay business is on the senior housing side, but with a margin that is correspondingly half or 1/3 of what the senior housing margin would be. So the NOI works out to, on a per bed basis back of the napkin kind of roughly similar.
So you're seeing good NOI growth and maintained NOI numbers, but you might see a more nuanced thing on the revenue side of Trilogy, where there's a mix shift happening where there's more people in senior housing beds at a lower revenue rate than there are on the skilled nursing side, and it looks like a decel in revenue when actually it's just Trilogy's business as usual. To the overarching question of how can Trilogy grow and how long can this last?
That is the question that we've been asked every quarter for the last 11 quarters and every quarter for the last 11 quarters, Trilogy has surprised us on how well they can continue to grow and the different levers that they find to grow. Part of that is the alignment, like Jeff said, not only do we have a great RIDEA contract, but we had -- we were the first people in the space to create an operator incentive equity plan where Trilogy's long-term incentive plan is actually paid in AHR stock. So they're riding the wave of the value creation at Trilogy and fully aligned to do that. I wouldn't bet against them.
Austin Wurschmidt: Yes. And we're going to keep asking you don't worry within the non-same-store pool portion of Trilogy, I mean, it's still half of Trilogy's overall portfolio. I think you're approaching about 1 year since you guys acquired the Kingston portfolio. You're adding IL Villas. How does the growth compare within that pool of assets relative to the same-store pool? And anything specific we should be thinking about as we head into next year?
Gabriel Willhite: Yes. So maybe the most undervalued part of our entire platform is Trilogy's development capabilities, right, and how that flows through in the Trilogy non-same-store. So we have Trilogy doing 3 to 5 new campuses a year of development. They're de-risked. Trilogy has built over 80 properties themselves, developed themselves, and they value engineered the prototype. So we get asked a lot of questions how can you actually still do development in Trilogy? How does it make sense when nobody else really is. That's part of the reason. It's the value engineering of the building, not only from a cost perspective from -- but also from an operations perspective.
It's taking -- stripping out the developer returns that are part of the development. And now Trilogy is actually doing their own general contractor work on some of the projects as well, which further takes the cost down. So as those enter the total portfolio pool when they come online, they do provide a growth opportunity that I think is going to be sustainable and repeatable over the long term. And like I said, 3 to 5 campuses a year is what Trilogy kind of -- you can expect from Trilogy.
But on top of that, we have over 30 campuses with excess land or a direct path to excess land where we can do campus expansions at Trilogy, which are typically private pay senior housing, either IL or memory care or assisted living expansions. Those have great returns, maybe smaller dollars attached to the overall project. On the Kingston portfolio, specifically, that's a deal that we closed at the end of 2025, where Trilogy is a great operator, is able to take over assets and start to implement their own operational plans in those assets. We're seeing really good progress within those buildings.
And I think they will fuel the -- they'll be -- they'll enter the same-store pool, I believe, next year, and they'll fuel some powerful same-store NOI growth next year as well.
Operator: Your next question is from Michael Lewis with Truist Securities.
Michael Lewis: I was hoping I'd be the one that asked the election question, so I could say the term bluenami, which I think is fun to say. Instead, I'm going to ask about acquisitions. You talked about going into new regions of the country, maybe higher quality and price per pound was up. So are going-in yield and expected stabilized yield changing because of the mix or maybe just because things got more expensive for levered buyers or for any reason? And a second part of that, how do you feel about the acquisitions you made prior to 3Q versus the product you're buying now? Would you still buy it today?
Stefan K. Oh: Thanks for the question, Michael. So I guess just to answer your second question first. I mean, obviously, we're very proud of the acquisitions that we did prior to 3Q. I mean maybe the Kensington portfolio and the LCB portfolio, maybe there's a different geographic layout and maybe a quality difference in terms of the build-out and such. But at the end of the day, all of the acquisitions we're doing are really based around what is the performance level, what is the -- what can the operator do in these properties? Are these long-term assets where they are going to be competitive for many years to come.
I think there's definitely with some of the assets that we've recently acquired a built-in fortress there where these markets are not going to be seeing a lot of supply increase -- it's just very difficult to build in these areas. There's a lot a long process that goes -- that has to happen for someone to do that. But at the end of the day, it's all a matter of what is the long-term performance that we can generate out of our entire portfolio. And I think we've built a very good mix of assets that are going to continue to do that.
To your first question about price per unit, I think, again, it just plays into where are we buying, what is the quality of the real estate, what is the age. But -- and again, what is the ability to actually build in those locations. We're just not going to see a whole lot. And these are very high-performing assets that are generating very good RevPOR based on the fact the quality is very high. The rates are very good. And they're serving a market that is for a more affluent customer. So that's just a factor of the type of assets, has nothing to do necessarily with the yields or the pricing.
All of that has remained consistent throughout our entire portfolio and all the acquisitions we've been doing recently. So that's not a function of us paying more or accepting less of a yield from these assets. And at the end of the day, too, even though maybe there's some of these assets that are being priced at a higher per unit, they're still all below replacement costs. So we know that they're good investments for us, and they're going to be protected investments as well.
Jeffrey Hanson: And Mike, Jeff here. Thanks, Stefan. I'd add the entire $3-plus billion for context here, that's closed year-to-date plus pipeline, the yields are consistent with everything that we've been communicating all year long, mid-5s to mid-6s initial stabilized real yields -- initial yields was stabilized above 7%. And with 2019 vintage, it's some of the highest quality, best located senior housing product in the country. And Stefan referred to high barrier to entry and also as a distinction, fortress markets.
What we mean by fortress markets is much of what we bought, not all, but much of what we bought this year is in fortress markets where it's 5 to 8 to 9 years concept to delivery because there is no developable land. You have to assemble parcels to go through the entitlement process and then develop or redevelop. And in terms of higher price per unit, the economics support it. Kensington is a perfect example. All those assets are in these fortress markets.
They're super high acuity, almost 100% -- well, 100% of 7 of those 8 assets, all 7 that they built, purpose-built for their plan is all AL and memory care with RevPOR between 16,000 to 26,000 units. So the economics are fully supported. And you've got not only additional occupancy lift in everything we're buying this year, but also enhanced pricing power with material barrier to entry -- barrier to entry, rather.
Gabriel Willhite: And one more thing we haven't touched on that I want to bring up because I think people are just getting this wrong by quoting price per unit too much. We're seeing the boomer generation wanting more space and focus on bigger units. So the price per unit that you might be thinking of historically in senior housing for a studio room is -- that is not what we're buying. We're buying the bigger units, which is where the demand is showing up the most. Many times, there's 2 bedroom units that people are wanting to move into.
So maybe we need to shift as an industry to start talking more about the price per square foot and how much amenity space there is and what those amenities look like because all of that goes into that per pound equation that we're talking about. So I think if you're out there buying studio AL right now, you may -- I like where we're positioned on a relative basis where we have more bedrooms, bigger units. Oftentimes, we have 2 bedrooms and they're highly amenitized buildings. I think that's where the demand is going to be the highest. We could be wrong. We could be making the wrong bet, of course, but I like where we're at.
Jeffrey Hanson: And everything we bought this year is still below replacement cost. So that's a good cross-check.
Michael Lewis: Great. Maybe I cheated, I asked a multipart question there. But my second question, given the cost of equity and the cost of debt, -- is it safe to assume you're going to fund all your capital needs with equity for the foreseeable future? And to the extent you could talk about it, how much forward equity capacity do you like to have in reserve at any given time?
Aric Chang: Mike, it's Aric. Great question. So I'll clarify one thing, like based on the visibility we have on the pipeline and then some, we don't have any plan to go out to the market. We are fully funded for that pipeline. To ask your question, whenever we do go to the market, we intend to have match-funded opportunities. So we are raising capital with identified accretive investments. Now in the terms of -- you asked about sort of capacity and what we like to have. Again, it would be based on the opportunities at hand.
Operator: Your next question is from Dave Rogers with Raymond James.
David Rodgers: Just one question for me to follow up on maintenance CapEx of Trilogy. It looks like it's growing much faster than the size of the portfolio. Just not sure if that was related to some acquisitions and deferred CapEx that you saw specifically there. And then maybe just a broader question around how much deferred CapEx are you seeing as you're looking at assets and as that acquisition pipeline for SHOP or within the Trilogy business continues to grow.
Aric Chang: Well, one thing is on the maintenance CapEx that we've disclosed, it's only on the total portfolio basis. So that is sort of a reflection of -- as we increased the portfolio in the campuses.
Gabriel Willhite: Yes. And not only that, that's spot on. Not only that, but the Kingston portfolio that we bought, we built in some maintenance CapEx into that, that we knew about when we came into the deal. So you're seeing that show up in the numbers as well.
Operator: Your next question is from Seth Bergey with Citi.
Seth Bergey: I just wanted to follow up with some of the kind of hiring that you've done and specifically on the technology side. Can you go into a little bit more detail on kind of what technology capabilities or initiatives that you'd kind of like to add to the platform that maybe you don't currently have?
Gabriel Willhite: Yes. It's a combination of enhancing what we already have and adding to it. So it's not just adding new things, it's making things better. We want market data and intel that our investments team can use to be a competitive advantage when we're evaluating sites. Some of that means tapping into the data that we already have to use it more efficiently. Some of that is looking at the alternative data sources where we feel like it's giving us an edge. We're looking at things that may be other -- may be different than what the world broadly is looking at.
On the asset management side, it's about further building out the connection points with our operators, so we have more insight faster into what's going on within the buildings beyond just the financial data that we're getting and really digging into the operational data so that we can give more insights and help them be better at executing their business plans. And it's layering on AI to those -- to all that data so that we can better use the data that we have. Jon Crosier, our new CTO, has been at the company for a little over 2 months now, and everybody is excited about the progress that we made in that short amount of time.
I think getting better on this front is really exciting right now. The senior housing business is one that rewards innovation, and it shows up in the NOI. So we're going to lean in and be innovators in the space, use the information that we have and use our new tech team to help drive total portfolio performance.
Seth Bergey: Great. And then maybe just a second, I want to follow up on some of the comments you made earlier around kind of SHOP and Trilogy being the go-forward engines as a company and being not sellers of OM. -- would you kind of look to do that just kind of as you have been in terms of kind of one-off transactions as they arise? Or would you look to do that as a portfolio -- larger portfolio sale? And can you just talk about kind of the demand out there for outpatient medical and kind of the depth of the buyer pool that's out there for those types of assets?
Jeffrey Hanson: Yes. Thanks, Seth. This is Jeff. Look, we're opportunistic. As I've said before, I'll say it again, nothing's bolted down. It's a stable asset class. There's always -- the 35 years I've been in this business, there's always been strong demand from a variety of capital sources.
Operator: Your next question is from Nick Yulico from Scotiabank.
Nicholas Yulico: I just want to go back to the RevPOR growth in the third quarter in SHOP, 5.4%, that number that strengthened this year. I just want to make sure that there's not like a comp issue affecting that number this quarter, making it artificially high.
Gabriel Willhite: No, great question. That's not what's driving it. It's actual execution within each building operator by operator, building by building. And it's a focus on street rate, right? It's not one-off in-place increases that happened midyear. It's execution on especially the rent concession front. So as you get more occupied, it's not only do you have more pricing power on rate, but you should stop using rent concessions as much as well. So we actually took our rent concession number down 34% year-over-year because of a hyper focus on that. And that's kind of circling back to the question before on data and analytics and what are you providing to your operators and how do you leverage that?
It's many different operational data points that you're drawing from to say, hey, I think we've got an opportunity here. Let's go out and attack it. And the great thing about having great operators is when you bring those types of ideas to them, they actually can go out and execute.
Nicholas Yulico: Okay. Great. And then second question, Aric, for the balance sheet. I think you have the swaps maturing in January. I think the term loan as well. Just latest thoughts on refinancing.
Aric Chang: Yes. Great question. Obviously, with the maturity in January, we're working on that. Right now, we want to maintain flexibility and optionality there. So we'll get into exactly on '27 capital markets execution. One thing I will note is if you look at our Q, we did put in place a swap in October, and that's to hedge some of our floating rate exposure going into '27. It's basically effective in January '27 concurrently when the existing swaps mature and the term loan matures. So you know that we're being mindful of floating rate exposure and working on things.
Jeffrey Hanson: Yes. We're working on refi opportunities and alternatives now, and we'll advise accordingly.
Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I will now turn the call back to Jeff Hanson, Chairman and CEO, for closing remarks.
Jeffrey Hanson: Well, thank you, ladies and gentlemen, for your continued support and confidence, and we hope everybody has a great weekend.
Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you so much for attending. You may now disconnect.

item.content:encoded:
Bethesda, Maryland - November 01, 2026 - Keith Miller Counseling, a therapy practice in Bethesda, Maryland, offers premarital counseling for engaged couples as the busiest stretch of the year for proposals gets underway. The practice works with couples from Bethesda and across Montgomery County who want to prepare for marriage before the wedding.
Engagement season is starting
Proposals tend to cluster in the colder months. According to The Knot 2025 Real Weddings Study, about 47 percent of couples get engaged between November and February, and the wedding planning site describes engagement season as running roughly from Thanksgiving to Valentine's Day. The Knot also reports that the average engagement lasts about 15 months, which gives many newly engaged couples more than a year between the proposal and the wedding.
That window is often filled with venues, guest lists and budgets. For many couples, it is also a good time to talk through the less visible parts of a shared life before they marry.
What research shows about premarital education
Research suggests that preparation can make a difference. A 2006 study by Scott Stanley and colleagues, published in the Journal of Family Psychology and based on a survey of adults in Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas and Arkansas, found that couples who took part in premarital education had about 31 percent lower odds of divorce than couples who did not. Because the study was a survey, it shows an association rather than proof that counseling alone caused the difference.
How premarital counseling works at the practice
The practice's premarital counseling draws on three established couples therapy models: Imago Relationship Theory, Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy and the Gottman Method. Couples can choose among the practice's counselors and approaches.
Sessions focus on practical preparation. Couples work through what the practice calls a "baggage check," addressing issues before they can damage the relationship. They also identify weak communication habits and replace them with stronger ones, talk about outside social pressures that can strain a marriage, work through the most frustrating parts of the relationship, and learn to receive love from each other more fully.
Conversations worth having before the wedding
Counseling before marriage gives couples a structured place to discuss topics that can be hard to raise on their own, such as how each partner handles money, how they will divide household responsibilities, what they expect from extended family, whether and when to have children, and how each of them reacts during an argument. Talking these through with a counselor can surface differences early, while the couple still has time to work on them together.
Scheduling for busy couples in Bethesda
Sessions run 50 minutes and take place at the practice's Bethesda office at 4300 Montgomery Avenue, which serves couples from Bethesda, Chevy Chase, Rockville, Silver Spring and other nearby communities. Evening and weekend appointments are available, which can help couples fit counseling around work and wedding planning.
Frequently asked questions
When should engaged couples start premarital counseling?
There is no single right time, but with engagements averaging about 15 months, many couples have time to start well before the wedding rather than in the final weeks.
Do couples need to be having problems to benefit?
No. Premarital counseling is preventive. It is designed to help couples build skills and talk through expectations before conflicts become entrenched.
What topics does premarital counseling cover at Keith Miller Counseling?
Sessions address unresolved issues each partner brings, communication habits, outside pressures on the relationship and the most frustrating parts of the relationship.
Is premarital counseling covered by insurance?
The practice is not in network with health plans. Many clients submit claims to their insurer as out-of-network care and receive partial reimbursement, which the practice says is often 40 to 60 percent, depending on the plan.
Where can couples attend premarital counseling in Bethesda?
Couples meet at the practice's Bethesda office at 4300 Montgomery Avenue, Suite 302. Evening and weekend appointments are available.
About Keith Miller Counseling
Founded in 2007 by Keith Miller, Keith Miller Counseling is a therapy practice based in Bethesda, Maryland, providing individual, couples and family therapy. The practice offers premarital and couples counseling, counseling for Black couples, Internal Family Systems (IFS) therapy, counseling for anxiety and trauma, and IQ and aptitude testing. Its mission is to help clients build healthier relationships and stronger mental health through evidence-based, culturally informed care. The practice serves clients throughout Montgomery County and the Washington, D.C. area and offers a free phone consultation to new clients.
