Lioness Star Thad Luckinbill Played Kaley Cuoco's Boyfriend On A Hit Sitcom
Long before Thad Luckinbill stepped into the role of Kyle on "Lioness," he played Kaley Cuoco's boyfriend on a hit sitcom. We're talking about Luckenbill's role as Donny Doyle on "8 Simple Rules," which was originally titled "8 Simple Rules ... for Dating My Teenage Daughter." Donny played the romantic interest of Cuoco's character, Bridget Hennessy.
Luckinbill's first appearance on "8 Simple Rules" (one of Cuoco's best TV shows) was Season 1, Episode 26, titled "The Doyle Wedding." The episode revolves around the Hennessy family — led by Paul Hennessy (John Ritter) — attending a wedding of their neighbors, the Doyles. It also serves as the very beginning of Bridget's romantic spark with Donny. Although she first used to think Donny was a little bit of a dork, she sees him in a new light during the ep.
Luckinbill's last appearance was Season 2, Episode 3, titled "Donny Goes AWOL" — and a lot of big things happen in between. In addition to Donny returning to the Naval Academy, Bridget now has another romantic interest to juggle. She also uses a video postcard set up by Donny's family to break up with him, leading to drama. "Donny Goes AWOL" is notable most of all because it served as Ritter's last appearance before his tragic, untimely death.
Thad Luckinbill also dated Kaley Cuoco
Thad Luckinbill and Kaley Cuoco didn't just play sweethearts on TV — they also dated in real life. According to Us Weekly, they were romantically linked in 2002. That said, not much is known about their relationship, or the reason why it ultimately ended. There are a few press photos of the pair posing together on red carpets, and not much else.
As of 2026, both Cuoco and Luckinbill are worlds away from their early '00s romance. Luckinbill, for his part, has been married to Amelia Heinle, his "The Young and the Restless" co-star, since 2007. They have two children. And although Luckinbill initiated divorce proceedings in 2017, they've since reconciled and are enjoying marital bliss, per Hello!.
Meanwhile, Cuoco is currently in a relationship with her fiancé, actor Tom Pelphrey. In October 2026, she gave birth to their second child together. "Philomena Carmine Bobby Pelphrey ... 10/12/26," Cuoco posted to Instagram. "There are no words to describe this feeling once again. What a blessing." She continued, "We are so grateful for the crazy wild up and down journey that brought us to our little Philo. Family officially complete. Time to bring Matilda's baby home! @tommypelphrey life exploded the minute we met, and the gifts keep coming."

Singer Soyou, a former member of the group SISTAR, shared her thoughts on cohabitation before marriage.
On the 19th, a video titled "Wow. You're really bad... | Soyou's Gossip Counseling Office 'Dating' Edition" was uploaded to Soyou's YouTube channel, "Soyouki."
Soyou spent time answering dating-related consultations sent in by her subscribers.
One subscriber shared their dilemma: "My boyfriend doesn't want to get married but wants to cohabit. He wants us to buy a home together, with him covering more of the cost and putting it in my name. I don't necessarily have to get married, so should we cohabit?"
In response, Soyou answered "Yes" without hesitation. Soyou said, "My boyfriend doesn't necessarily want to get married but wants to cohabit. He's paying more of the cost and putting it in my name—doesn't that show trust in me? Putting something in someone's name isn't easy. That is love."
Soyou added, "I am a proponent of cohabitation before marriage. There are already plus points to this. When you cohabit, you start to notice things about each other that are different, and there is also the fun of adjusting to those differences."
She continued, "If everything matches up, you end up getting married. You start thinking about marriage. But unless you dislike it when your boyfriend says, 'I will absolutely never get married. I will only cohabit,' I think it would be fine to cohabit. It's just dating for a long time and then moving in together, isn't it?"
Meanwhile, Soyou was born in September 1991 and is 35 years old by Korean age reckoning.

Al Masraf (Arab Bank for Investment & Foreign Trade) has announced that it has inked a major project financing deal with Innovo Group, an industry leader in construction and development across the built environment. This funding will help Innovo in delivering a significant project.
The agreement reflects Al Masraf’s continued commitment to supporting major businesses and projects that contribute to the UAE’s economic growth and development.
The agreement represents one of the largest project financing facilities Al Masraf has extended to a corporate client, highlighting the bank’s growing capability to provide tailored financing solutions for complex, strategically significant projects.
The media ceremony, held at Innovo Group’s head office in Dubai, brought together Fuad Mohamed, Chief Executive Officer of Al Masraf, and Bishoy Azmy, Chief Executive Officer of Innovo Group, to mark the milestone and highlight the organisations’ collaboration.
Speaking on the occasion, Mohamed said: "This milestone reflects Al Masraf’s commitment to supporting the UAE’s ambitious infrastructure and development agenda and to building long-term partnerships with leading organisations across the country."
"Our collaboration with Innovo Group demonstrates the strength of our corporate banking capabilities and our ability to provide tailored financing solutions that support projects of strategic importance. We are proud to play a role in enabling the delivery of major developments and look forward to strengthening our partnership with Innovo Group as we continue to support its growth and ambitions," he stated.
The project financing agreement underscores Al Masraf’s commitment to empowering future legacies by supporting businesses and projects that contribute to the UAE’s continued growth and long-term prosperity.
On the deal, Azmy said: "Al Masraf has been a valued banking partner to Innovo, and we welcome the opportunity to deepen our engagement. As our business evolves, we see scope to broaden our collaboration and work together on new opportunities."
Through its Corporate Banking business, Al Masraf continues to strengthen its role as a trusted financial partner to businesses contributing to the UAE’s economic development, providing tailored solutions designed around the needs and ambitions of its corporate clients.
"We look forward to building on the strong foundations of our relationship in the period ahead," he added.-TradeArabia News Service

item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Friday sought responses from the Centre and other authorities on a petition seeking uniform procedural safeguards and guidelines for all forms of 'talaq' (divorce) under Muslim personal law.
A bench comprising Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi was informed by the petitioner's counsel that the plea also challenges the validity of 'Talaq-e-Hasan'.
'Talaq-e-Hasan' is a form of divorce under which a Muslim man can end his marriage by pronouncing the word 'talaq' once a month over three months.
The bench also tagged the petition with a separate pending plea filed by a Muslim woman challenging the validity of 'Talaq-e-Hasan' pronounced by her husband.
The fresh petition has sought a direction to the authorities to declare 'Talaq-e-Hasan' and other forms of unilateral extra-judicial 'talaq' an evil that needs to be banned.
It has also sought adequate economic and social protection for divorced women and their children affected by arbitrary forms of 'talaq'. The petition seeks these measures to be provided retrospectively and on an ongoing basis.
The petition has urged the Centre to "frame and implement uniform procedural safeguards and legally enforceable guidelines governing all forms of 'talaq'/divorce under Muslim personal law, so as to ensure fairness, reconciliation, transparency and protection of the fundamental rights of women guaranteed under Articles 14, 15 and 21 of the Constitution".
It has also sought a direction to declare Section 2 of the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937, unconstitutional to the extent that it recognises and validates 'Talaq-e-Hasan' as a valid form of divorce.
The plea has further urged the Centre to frame comprehensive, gender-just and religion-neutral procedural safeguards for the dissolution of marriages, including divorce under personal laws.
It said these safeguards should be in line with Articles 14, 15 and 21 of the Constitution, which deal with equality before the law, protection against discrimination and the right to life and personal liberty.
While Article 14 pertains to equality before law, Article 15 deals with prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. Article 21 pertains to protection of life and personal liberty.
The plea has sought to declare that "absence of statutory safeguards regulating polygamy under Muslim personal law, insofar as it permits a Muslim man to contract multiple marriages without ensuring equality, dignity, informed consent, financial security and constitutional protection to the existing wife/wives, is arbitrary, discriminatory and violative of Articles 14, 15 and 21 of the Constitution".
It also sought a declaration that contracting a subsequent marriage without the free, prior and informed consent of the existing spouse, by concealing or suppressing such intention, is arbitrary and unconstitutional.
Under 'Talaq-e-Hasan', a divorce gets formalised after the third utterance of the word 'talaq' in the third month if cohabitation has not resumed during this period.
However, if cohabitation resumes after the first or second utterance of talaq, the parties are assumed to have reconciled.
In 2017, the top court declared triple 'talaq', also a form of divorce prevalent among the Muslim community, as unconstitutional after finding it to be arbitrary and violative of the fundamental rights of women.
(With inputs from news agency PTI)

item.content:encoded:
VATICAN CITY (OSV News) — On the third day of a weeklong Vatican meeting on marriage and family Oct. 9, Catholic bishops grappled with a trend that worries many Church leaders: young couples choosing to live together rather than wed.
“We cannot ignore the fact that the number of marriages is currently declining throughout the world, both civil marriages and marriages celebrated in the Church,” Cardinal Kevin Farrell, prefect of the Dicastery for Laity, Family, and Life said as he opened the day’s discussion.
The cardinal noted the concern of many Christian parents today “whose children suffer from loneliness, remain hesitant to make a lasting commitment, or categorically reject the path that their parents themselves had embraced with joy.”
The third day of the Oct. 7-14 gathering of the world’s bishops’ conference presidents and the heads of Eastern Catholic churches marking the 10th anniversary of “Amoris Laetitia” was devoted entirely to “young people and the discovery of the vocation to marriage.”
Auxiliary Bishop Stephen Eustace Victor Fernandes of Bombay, one of 26 experts invited to contribute to the discussions, was one of two featured speakers at the morning plenary session Oct. 9.
How Church can accompany couples living together outside marriage
Bishop Fernandes addressed how the Church can accompany couples who live together outside marriage. He urged bishops to avoid both indifference and condemnation, emphasizing the importance of listening to young people to understand their experiences and concerns.
Listening, he said, “enables us to distinguish between a rejection of marriage and a fear that lifelong committed love may no longer be possible.”
That distinction is particularly important for young people who have experienced family breakdown, separation, violence, abandonment or failed relationships, he said. Their reluctance to marry may reflect both emotional wounds and genuine questions about commitment.
“The first task is to know their story: Why have they chosen to live together? What do they hope for? What fears or obstacles stand before them? What is already good in their relationship?” Bishop Fernandes said.
“But accompaniment must also involve genuine discernment. The question is not simply: How can we move this couple towards a wedding? It is also: Are these two people truly called to marriage, and are they ready to enter into a lifelong marital covenant? Some cohabiting relationships may contain authentic love and important elements of commitment, while still lacking the conditions necessary for a mature marital covenant,” he added.
Stressing importance of forming young people in virtues
Bishop Fernandes also stressed the importance of forming young people in the virtues that sustain marriage, including fidelity, responsibility, chastity, forgiveness, perseverance, generosity and openness to life.
That formation involves teaching young people to communicate, resolve conflict, apologize and forgive, he said, while helping them understand that love depends not only on emotion but also on repeated decisions to seek the good of another person.
“Rather than presenting Christian morality primarily in terms of prohibitions and obligations, we need to speak of love as gift, freedom as self-giving, sexuality as the person’s capacity to love and give oneself, fidelity as the foundation of trust and stability, and marriage as a covenant capable of giving meaning to life,” he said.
Archbishop Timothy Costelloe of Perth, Australia, also addressed the issue of cohabitation, saying many young people no longer understand or accept the traditional Christian connection between sexuality, marriage and procreation.
He pointed to the influence of social media, entertainment and online culture, which often emphasize personal fulfillment and autonomy over permanence and sacrifice.
“We are competing with many other approaches to the meaning of marriage,” he said.
Meeting cohabiting couples where they are
“Although young couples who live together before marrying are falling short of the ideal of Christian marriage, this does not mean that there is nothing good in their relationships: we met them where they are and accompany them as they move forward to a fuller expression of the Christian ideal,” Archbishop Costelloe added.
Speaking with OSV News after the morning session, Archbishop Costelloe said Australia’s highly secular culture continues to make it difficult for the Church to engage deeply in people’s lives.
He recommended that if local parish communities can discover ways in which the witness of married couples and families can be both visible and celebrated, the fear of commitment and doubts about permanence which trouble many young people might be mitigated to some extent.
“As one married couple explained to me, The most persuasive argument for Christian marriage is often a married couple living it well,” he said.
Among the 11 married couples from around the world invited to share their testimonies with the bishops are Charmaine Bernadette Villegas and Eren Lyle Villegas from the Philippines who are serving as missionaries in Rome with the Couples for Christ apostolate.
Offering example of Christian marriage rather than impose beliefs
In their work with couples who live together, the Villegases said they seek to offer an example of Christian marriage rather than impose their beliefs.
“We don’t want to force who we are as a married couple, but just simply living out as a witness of what we believe marriage is, and in the hope that they too will see it the way we see it,” Eren Lyle Villegas told OSV News.
Charmaine Bernadette Villegas said many young people in the Philippines are postponing marriage rather than rejecting it outright. Some want to establish their careers first, while others face economic pressures and believe they need financial stability before marrying.
The couple, who have been married for 16 years and do not have children, said they continue to pray for a family while embracing what they describe as a call to serve as spiritual parents to young people in their parish and community.
“We’ve been praying since day one, but we have always believed that the Lord is faithful. And in his perfect timing will answer that prayer,” Eren said.
Gathering’s format outlined during a briefing
Father Giacomo Costa, a consultant to the General Secretariat of the Synod who oversees the meeting’s methodology, outlined the gathering’s format during an Oct. 9 briefing at the Holy See Press Office.
Participants are divided into 16 small groups seated at round tables in the Paul VI Hall, using the “conversation in the spirit” method employed during the Synod on Synodality, he said.
The groups reflect the global reach of the Church, Father Costa said. Italian-speaking groups, for example, include participants from China, Poland, Mexico, Central Asia, Greece, Bulgaria, Slovenia, Germany and Croatia.
Each of the 16 groups approved a report and presented it to the wider assembly during the afternoon plenary session, he said.
Discussions during the meeting’s first days also addressed the formation of seminarians who grew up in a digital culture and, in some cases, in blended families. Participants considered how those experiences shape seminarians’ understanding of relationships and how formation programs can help them understand their own histories and learn to accompany others, Father Costa said.
Another focus was the meaning of accompaniment and the practical steps needed to make it effective.
“We asked ourselves how we can bridge the gap between the desire to be close and to accompany and the actual capacity to do so?” Father Costa said.
Church must consider who is equipped to accompany people
Accompaniment risks becoming a concept that participants endorse in principle without a clear understanding of how to put it into practice, he said. The Church must consider who is equipped to accompany people, what preparation is needed and how to respond to different situations.
The Vatican also announced the members of the commission responsible for preparing the meeting’s summary report, which is expected to be published Oct. 14, the final day of the gathering.
The commission includes Cardinal Pablo Virgilio Siongco David of the Philippines; Cardinal Mario Grech; Cardinal Matteo Zuppi; Archbishop José Manuel Imbamba of Angola; Philippe Bordeyne, president of the Pontifical John Paul II Theological Institute for Marriage and Family Sciences; and Orietta Rachele Grazioli, a professor at the institute.
The bishops are scheduled to turn their attention to the first years of marriage during the weekend discussions. Spanish Cardinal José Cobo Cano and Argentine theologian María Marcela Mazzini are scheduled to address the gathering on Oct. 10 before the bishops take Sunday off as a day of rest.
Courtney Mares is Vatican editor for OSV News. Follow her on X @catholicourtney.

item.content:encoded:
A new wedding trends survey reveals that almost two thirds (62 per cent) of people in Brighton would opt for a ‘phone-free’ wedding, suggesting uninterrupted and meaningful ceremonies are on the rise.
The research, conducted by the engagement ring experts at Austen & Blake comes from a survey they ran of 1000 respondents in the UK to reveal the wedding traditions of 2026.
As wedding planning continues to evolve, the findings provide insight into the priorities, values, and emerging trends reshaping modern celebrations.
The outdated wedding and proposal traditions
According to the survey, over a third of people in Brighton (35 per cent) think that the three month spending rule on engagement rings is outdated and asking parental permission before proposing should be a thing of the past (22 per cent).
The wedding traditions Brighton would most likely get rid of:
When it comes to the wedding day, the people of Brighton think parents paying for the wedding is the tradition they would most likely get rid of (30 per cent), followed by the first dance (19 per cent).
The wedding tradition that’s here to stay in Brighton!
The research shows that the wedding tradition that is here to stay in Brighton is having bridesmaids and groomsmen. A huge 90 per cent of Brighton think this is the most important tradition and the least likely to be replaced any time soon.
AI takes a front seat
Although the new trend of ‘phone free’ weddings has emerged from the research, the use of technology when it comes to preparing for proposals and weddings is still a top priority for Brits.
According to the research, 19 per cent of people in Brighton would use AI to organise the perfect proposal, and 16 per cent would use AI to write their wedding vows.
AI is also taking a front seat when it comes to wedding planning, with digital wedding planning including the use of apps and AI (32 per cent) taking over traditional forms of planning such as wedding journals (18 per cent) and wedding planners (18 per cent).
Wedding guest etiquette
The survey also reveals what UK respondents feel is the worst wedding etiquette, proving that there are traditions and ‘unspoken’ rules when it comes to the big day. Drinking too much is considered to be the worst wedding etiquette in Brighton.
- Drinking too much — 19 per cent
- Bringing an uninvited plus one — 19 per cent
- Posting on social media without permission — 16 per cent
- Joining in on the first dance — 16 per cent
- Wearing white as a guest — 11 per cent
How does Brighton feel about destination weddings abroad in 2026?
With more travel-led weddings happening than ever before, the jewellery specialists asked Brighton how they feel about attending weddings abroad.
When asked which statement best describes their view on destination weddings, over a third (38 per cent) said they are stressful and expensive for guests, while 24 per cent cited them as a fun excuse for a holiday, and 16 per cent would describe them as fun and romantic.

item.content:encoded:
From floral arrangements featuring poppies and hydrangeas to unconventional venue choices, 2027 weddings will be filled with personal touches and unexpected moments. That’s according to the latest findings from The Knot.
The wedding planning site just released its 2027 Wedding Trends Report, a look at what’s growing in popularity among couples right now.
To compile the list, the editors at The Knot reviewed dozens of trending wedding concepts that they believed could result in widespread adoption across weddings in 2027. Those predictions were then validated by a pre-selected group of wedding vendors from The Knot Vendor Marketplace. Additionally, to provide comprehensive insights, The Knot Worldwide analyzed on-site behavioral data through June 2026, in addition to existing data on its U.S. audience of pre-engaged and engaged couples.
Here are the top 20 wedding trends that are expected to dominate 2027.
Sophisticated Colors
Primary color palettes for 2027 nuptials are predicted to incorporate shades like regal merlot, plums, powdery blues, and moss greens. Secondary colors to supplement these bold hues include blush pinks and champagnes. The Knot reports a 127 percent increase year-over-year in this trend.
Antique Lace
According to The Knot editors, lace is no longer limited to bridal gowns and veils, noting a 280 percent year-over-year increase in the look. The vintage-style fabric is now dressing up wedding stationery, as well as tablescapes and décor. “Lace nods to vintage beauty and antique design, yet it feels modern at the same time,” planner Danielle Elder of Classic Events says in the report.
The Beach Club
Engaged couples are exploring ways to bring the Amalfi Coast to their weddings back home, according to the report. The Knot points to design ideas like spritz bars for cocktail hour, cabana stripes across patio furniture, lemon-embellished tablescapes and stationery, and textiles steeped in sun-dappled marigolds and Mediterranean blues.
“Couples planning multi-day experiences want to incorporate a fun poolside or oceanfront experience for their guests,” says designer and planner Jason Rhee of Rheefined Company. “I also think with Italy being a trendy destination, it’s becoming an inspiration piece for many couples.” The trend has seen a whopping 315 percent increase in interest.
Swans & Balletcore
More couples are taking pointers from Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake and embellishing their weddings with swan motifs and other balletcore elements such as ribbons, loose bows, textured draping, and crystal, The Knot editors found.
Related Stories
Monofloral Installations
More submissions are coming into The Knot‘s Real Wedding section that include hydrangea, moss, or wisteria installations. Depending on the flower type, single floral designs can be more impactful than mixed arrangements, with the report revealing that the concept is trending up. “The look is tailored, organic, and neat, but messy and almost like a still-life painting,” Elder says. “Antique hydrangea is having a huge comeback.”
Whimsical Florals
Whimsical flowers, in particular the poppy, are gaining popularity, as are other blooms that present a similar aesthetic. It’s all about playful petals.
The Silver (Ag)e
Silver (or Ag, as its abbreviation on the Periodic Table of elements) is making a fresh comeback. The sterling transition metal is influencing wedding accessories, stationery, dinnerware, and flatware, according to the report. “The silver accents we’ve seen to date feel like a fun meshing of vintage charm and modern elegance,” says Micaela Erickson, director of marketing at Vesper, citing examples like “vintage silver trays holding lighters, cigarettes, and other vices for guests to indulge in, eclectic mirrors with the couple’s monogram, and almost futuristic silver floral arrangements.”
The Arts as Inspiration
The arts, including photography, painting, music, sculpture, and more, are influencing the creative direction of weddings even more lately, including venue choices. “I’m seeing the arts pop up in engagement shoots. Couples are also leaning toward art museums and libraries, and including stained glass pieces, particularly, in their welcome signage,” says Lexsey Lanzotti of Zotti & Co.
Unconventional Venues
Within the last year, The Knot editors and their consulting vendors have seen weddings hosted at beach clubs, members clubs, townhomes, spas, and even sports arenas. “I think people are really starting to venture out and do things their own way,” Lanzotti says.
The Wedding Brand
A wedding’s iconography is now easily identifiable from the moment a guest receives a save-the-date and opens up the couple’s wedding website. Custom crests, bespoke illustrations, and personalized pieces as part of a branding puzzle are in demand. “We like to say it’s akin to a leitmotif in an opera or a piece of music. It’s a consistent thread that helps tell the story through melodies rather than words,” Elder says.
Prop Surrealism
The Knot notes that more couples are now requesting unexpected texture for their backdrops, design layouts, and more. “This is a fun opportunity for couples to showcase their taste, creativity, and interests,” Erickson says. “It’ll result in exciting, playful photo moments for couples and guests, and subvert more traditional wedding expectations.”
Interior Design Weddings
Lately, couples want their guests to feel “at home,” according to The Knot, so they’re creating a wedding environment that reflects their residential preferences. Table lamps, menu tassels, and even coffee table guest books offer the look of a luxurious interior space.
The Pop-Up … Plus
Moving beyond merch, wedding favors are now full-blown pop-up experiences—something that guests can enjoy in the moment and take home to savor. Think a fragrance station, a bouquet bar, or espresso martini service.
Playing With Food and Interactive F&B
Interactive food and beverage options are giving couples and wedding guests permission to play with their food. “We’re planning a secret pickle bar in the vault of the wedding venue,” says Carly Katz-Hackman, partner at Pinch Food Design, about an upcoming wedding planned by Pinch. “Think pickleback shots, pickled onion martinis, plus all the crunchy goodness you can imagine. Who needs bar nuts when you can have pickles?”
Cultural Menus
According to The Knot research, 60 percent of couples find it important to incorporate ethnicity, religion, and/or culture into their weddings. This is translating into menus that are deeply personal and meaningful. “We’ve definitely seen a ton of requests to infuse the couple’s culture into their wedding menu to show not only where they come from as individuals, but how they plan to move forward as a couple,” Katz says. “Whether it’s an Indian station for him, plus a Maryland station for her, and a New York station for them; or a full Chinese banquet dinner, plus challah made by the mother of the bride…We’re seeing worlds collide in the best way.”
Editorial-Cinematic Photos
Couples want to feel like the main character on their big day, and they’re using photography to give them the cinematic treatment, The Knot reports. “The photo requests that I’m seeing most right now are for images to feel emotional,” Lanzotti says. “Instead of standard, posed photos, couples want it to feel dreamy, romantic, artsy… People are really into creative composition lately.”
Experiential Stationery
In 2027, expect couples to get even more creative about their paper products—from save-the-dates to escort cards. According to the report, inspiration ranges from custom illustrations and handwritten lettering to pop-up designs on menus and wedding ceremony program fans. “There’s a definite shift towards hyper curation; for both documentation and immortalization,” Erickson says. “The desire to make aesthetics bold, unique, and highly tailored has never been stronger.”
Analog Registries
What’s old is new again, especially when it comes to wedding registries. Couples are seeking old-school cocktail glasses, camcorders, hip retro appliances, and vintage-style record players with modern capabilities as gifts.
Hush-Hush Honeymoons
Tougher-to-access resorts and destinations are gaining interest among couples, The Knot reports. Private villa resorts and ultra-luxury hotels offer a scenic escape from crowds, especially in romantic hotspots like Santorini, the Amalfi Coast, and Ibiza. Alternatively, lesser-known islands across the Mediterranean that require an extra ferry ride are worth the journey to some. Ships are another out-of-the-way choice.
Extending the Wedding
With the revival of courthouse ceremonies and the growth in welcome parties, couples are maximizing every wedding moment. “A wedding weekend is not just a celebration of two people anymore, where the focus is solely inward,” Elder says. “Couples now want that energy, love, and goodness pointed outward to experience and share with their guests.”

item.content:encoded:
California Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 1267 (Pellerin, D-Santa Cruz) on Wednesday, banning child marriage in the state.
The bill, sponsored by Unchained at Last and the California Commission on the Status of Women and Girls, repeals provisions that allowed a minor to enter into a marriage or domestic partnership with parental consent. It sets the state's minimum marriage and domestic partnership age at 18. Seventeen U.S. states have completely banned child marriage without exception.
Newsom signed the bill in his office with advocate Courtney Stodden, a survivor whose parents allowed her to marry 50-year-old actor Doug Hutchison when she was 16. Stodden has described the relationship as abusive and predatory, and it drew widespread public scrutiny. Since her divorce, she has publicly struggled with chronic depression and suicide attempts, and has become a national leader in the fight against child exploitation.
"This is a long overdue measure to protect young Californians and minors. Today, California kids are safer than ever before," Newsom said.
"Governor Newsom's action today made clear to me and to survivors of child marriage everywhere that we should never have been expected to carry this burden," Stodden said. "I'm deeply grateful to Unchained At Last and every survivor who fought to make this possible — California is a victory, but I'm not stopping here. I will keep fighting until children are protected from marriage in all 50 states."
"The heart of this effort has always been the survivors," said Assemblymember Gail Pellerin. "They told us what it means to be a child in a marriage you did not freely choose. They told us about coercion and abuse hidden behind the appearance of consent. They told us how difficult it can be for a minor to ask for help, find an attorney, leave home, or escape the very adults who are supposed to protect them. Because of them, California children are safer."

item.content:encoded:
TOKYO — True love may be priceless. But in Japan, 20-somethings are flocking to marriage agencies that promise a fast track to the altar — and charge a premium for it.
For hundreds of years, through the post-World War II era, Japanese marriages were brokered through “omiai,” a practice in which matchmakers — usually relatives, family friends, or bosses — linked singles in their orbit. But the custom fell out of fashion, giving way to organic dating and, eventually, a wave of casual-dating apps.
Now, young adults are enrolling at record rates in marriage agencies, where counselors serve as professional matchmakers. Across Tokyo, advertisements line metro cars, urging commuters to “leave life’s fateful encounters to the pros.” Another declares: “Better one omiai than 100 swipes.”
Experts say the shift is being driven by a backlash against frustrations familiar to modern daters globally. With social circles shrinking, young Japanese — tired of the ghosting, catfishing, and noncommittal matches rampant on dating apps — are turning to hands-on human guidance for greater efficiency and assurance.
Among the new recruits was Taizen Yasuda. A soft-spoken 28-year-old, he said he had run out of patience for algorithm-driven romance.
“The process of endless matching, messaging, and finally meeting on apps was exhausting,” Yasuda said. Matchmaking services, he thought, “would be the quickest way to find someone with the exact same goal — marriage.”
The practice is resurging as Japan grapples with a shrinking population and fewer young families. Because childbearing in Japan remains overwhelmingly tied to marriage, encouraging more people to wed has become part of the country’s broader push to boost its birth rate.
One company has positioned itself at the center of the matchmaking trend: IBJ, a Tokyo-based giant with a nationwide network. Promising to take clients from first meeting to proposal in three months, the company has seen membership and profits soar. It now claims a hand in roughly 1 of every 25 marriages in Japan.
Yasuda is part of a wave of young singles who have joined IBJ. On a recent Sunday, he sat across from his counselor in a quiet consultation room, clad in a stiffly pressed suit, with a sweep of wavy hair combed to the side. A little more than a month after joining the matchmaking service, Yasuda had already narrowed his prospects to two women. He had just taken one on a weekend drive to see a field of yellow canola blooms.
Every member is assigned a consultant who micromanages the courtship process. The consultants advise on everything from grooming and messaging etiquette to date itineraries.
When two members match, their consultants work in tandem behind the scenes, doing what they call “Cupid work” — exchanging and filtering postdate feedback and helping orchestrate every milestone, down to an eventual proposal.
“We are providing the kind of support only humans can offer to help people get married as quickly as possible,” said Shigeru Ishizaka, IBJ’s chief executive.
In an increasingly digitized society, “there is a deep desire to have a person guiding you through the process of dating,” said Junko Yamada, a lecturer at Tokai University in Tokyo who studies the psychology of romance. Echoing the reassurance of traditional omiai, she said having an expert curate matches offered psychological safety.
Yamada said that today’s youths seemed fixated on maximizing efficiency in every aspect of their lives and that these agencies appealed to that mindset by filtering out people who weren’t serious about marriage.
IBJ’s network of affiliated marriage agencies has varying costs and eligibility rules. Members typically pay about $30 to $100 a month, an enrollment fee of $650 to $1,300, and an additional $1,300 “success fee” if a couple get engaged. It also charges a $1,300 fee if couples violate its rules against “banned activities,” including premarital sex and cohabitation. IBJ said its counselors tracked the progression of their clients’ relationships.
Enrollment is generally limited to applicants with steady incomes. IBJ’s largest directly operated agency accepts only women ages 20 to 39 and men ages 25 to 49.
Critics argue that corporate services like IBJ, a company listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange with annual revenue exceeding $130 million, strip the soul from traditional matchmaking, impose rigid timelines on anxious young adults, and turn dating into a moneymaking endeavor.
Among the skeptics is Ikuko Kato, a veteran matchmaker who operates from her lace-curtained home just outside Tokyo, filled with hundreds of smiling pictures of couples she has matched. Dressed in pearls and a pink knit suit, Kato said she had matched more than 1,300 couples over 44 years and claimed that not a single pair had divorced.
“They’re too focused on business,” said Kato, who also charges clients a monthly fee as well as a fee if her matchmaking results in marriage. “My parents were neighborhood matchmakers. It’s in my blood. Modern corporate agents cannot do what I do.”
Unlike neighborhood matchmakers, IBJ moves clients through a lucrative, end-to-end program. Beyond matchmaking, its group companies offer wedding planning, financial consulting, and housing services, along with referrals to affiliated businesses like eyebrow-grooming salons.
Membership has grown about 50 percent over the past five years, and IBJ reported a 44 percent jump in first-half revenue this year, to about $91 million.
Ishizaka, the chief executive, said he viewed IBJ’s mission as more than just money. When he left banking and entered the matchmaking industry in 2000, he said, he hoped to reverse Japan’s severe demographic decline.
“Since Japanese society rarely conceives children outside of wedlock, I realized a matching service specifically focused on marriage would have a vital future,” he said.
Recently, that mission got a dose of encouraging news. In the first six months of 2026, births in Japan rose 0.8 percent, the first increase in 11 years for that period, according to the Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare. The modest uptick followed two straight years of increased marriages.
Yasuda, the IBJ client, said he hoped to contribute to those numbers. Part of his desire to marry quickly, he said, comes from wanting to start early enough to raise three or four children.
Ishizaka sees clients like Yasuda as evidence that a generation frequently portrayed as retreating from marriage may instead be looking for a more efficient route toward it.
“Surveys consistently show that over 80 percent of young people say they want to marry if they find the right partner,” he said. “I am certain that every married couple we create contributes directly to reversing the birth rate decline.”
This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

item.content:encoded:
When the unthinkable happens and a loved one is lost due to the negligence or misconduct of another, the right to seek justice falls primarily on the shoulders of immediate family members. In the realm of wrongful death claims, spouses, children and parents of unmarried children are often at the forefront, bearing the legal status to act as primary plaintiffs. This hierarchy of claimants is not just a legal formality; it reflects the profound personal and economic losses these individuals suffer.
As the closest relatives, they are presumed to be the most affected by the absence of the deceased, both emotionally and financially, and the law recognizes their need for reparation.
Extended family and financial dependents
But what about the extended family and those who financially depended on the deceased? The rights of siblings, grandparents and even non-relatives who may have been financially reliant on the deceased can vary significantly. While not typically in the front line for claims, these individuals may still have the right to compensation under certain circumstances.
Understanding the nuances of who is entitled to file a wrongful death claim requires a careful examination of the relationship with the deceased and the financial impact of their loss. It's a complex area that underscores the importance of each case's unique details.
State-specific laws and statutes of limitations
Embarking on a wrongful death lawsuit is a journey that is navigated differently in every state. Each state carries its own set of rules and regulations that govern who is eligible to file a claim. This patchwork of laws means that what applies in one jurisdiction may not hold true in another, making local legal counsel not just helpful but essential.
For residents of Bulloch County and surrounding areas, understanding Georgia's specific wrongful death statutes is the first step in assessing the viability of a claim. It's a critical aspect that underscores the importance of consulting with a knowledgeable local attorney who can provide guidance tailored to the state's legal landscape.
Timeframe for filing a claim
Time is of the essence in wrongful death cases, as the law imposes strict deadlines known as statutes of limitations. These legal time limits dictate how long you have to file a claim, and missing this window can mean forfeiting your right to seek justice altogether. In Georgia, the statute of limitations for filing a wrongful death claim typically stands at two years from the date of death. This underscores the urgency of taking legal action promptly.
Proof of relationship and impact
Establishing a claim in a wrongful death lawsuit is not merely a matter of asserting a loss. Claimants must substantiate their relationship to the deceased and demonstrate the tangible impact the loss has had on their lives. This proof goes beyond blood ties; it encompasses the full spectrum of emotional and financial support that the deceased provided. This process may be more straightforward for immediate family members, but for others, it can be a complex legal challenge. The depth of the relationship, the extent of dependency, and the nature of support previously provided are all scrutinized to establish the legitimacy of a claim.
Exceptions and special circumstances
There are, however, exceptions and special circumstances that can alter who has the standing to sue for wrongful death. In some cases, individuals who are not immediate family members may be granted the right to file a claim if they can demonstrate a significant enough impact on their lives due to the death. This might include dependents who are not related by blood but were financially supported by the deceased, or even a life partner with whom there was a cohabitation arrangement. Understanding these exceptions is crucial, as they can open the door for additional claimants who otherwise might not have considered themselves eligible.

Mumbai, September 24 (IANS) Politician Raghav Chadha marked 3 years of marital bliss with Bollywood actress Parineeti Chopra with an adorable wish on social media.
Expressing his gratitude for the life the two of them are building together, Raghav uploaded a video montage of some rare moments of the lovebirds together on IG.
He wrote on the photo-sharing app, "Three years and I’m still not sure if I’ve found the words to describe how much you mean to me. Which is saying something, because I’m usually not short of them (sic)."
"From that first breakfast together to now, you have somehow made every version of life feel warmer, fuller and more like home. Particularly, this past year has given us so much to hold close, and somehow made me even more grateful for the life we are building together. Happy anniversary @parineetichopra (sic)," he added.
Raghav concluded the post, saying, "I feel incredibly lucky that I get to do life with you."
Parineeti's mother and Raghav's mother-in-law, Reena Chopra, wished the couple in the comment section, saying, "Awww !! Love you both! Happy Anniversary".
Parineeti and Raghav tied the knot on September 24, 2023, in a private ceremony in Udaipur.
The couple embraced parenthood on October 19, 2025, as they welcomed their son Neer.
These two are frequently seen supporting each other on social media.
Most recently, Raghav praised Parineeti ahead of her OTT debut with 'Shaque'.
Sharing the recently released trailer of 'Shaque' on his official Instagram handle, Raghav penned, “So proud of you @parineetichopra...I know how much you gave to Shaque, especially through a time that was already very special for us. Having spent some time at the shoot in Shimla, I also got to see the warmth and talent of the team behind it. An exceptionally talented bunch, and clearly one you had a lot of fun working with.”

La psychologie est claire : les personnes

qui dorment avec leur chien ou chat ne sont pas anxieuses, elles

partagent ces 3 traits qui en disent long

Votre chien envahit la moitié du lit, votre chat s'installe

contre votre oreiller ? On vous a peut-être déjà dit que cette

habitude trahissait un besoin d'être rassuré. Pourtant, dormir avec

son animal ne veut pas forcément dire que vous être anxieux ou que

vous vous sentez seul. La psychologie vous attribue 5 traits

particuliers.

17 % des Français dorment avec leur animal de compagnie, selon

une enquête INSV/MGEN.

Dormir avec un animal peut refléter un besoin de proximité

affective et une grande sensibilité.

La qualité du sommeil partagé avec un animal varie, influençant

différemment le repos des propriétaires.

Ce résumé généré par IA a

été validé par les journalistes de la rédaction.

Dormir avec son chien ou son chat est une

habitude partagée par bon nombre d’entre nous. Selon une

enquête INSV/MGEN menée par OpinionWay auprès de 1001 Français,

17 % des personnes ayant un animal de compagnie le laissent

dormir dans leur lit ou leur chambre chaque nuit. C’est

même, en réalité, l’une des habitudes de « co-dodo » les

plus courantes, aux côtés du couple et de l’enfant. Mais qu’est ce

que ce phénomène veut dire de vous ?

Selon YourTango,

plusieurs psychologues et thérapeutes observent des points communs

chez les personnes qui partagent leur lit avec leur

animal : un besoin de proximité

affective, une grande sensibilité et

empathie, ainsi qu’une certaine

tolérance aux petits désagréments nocturnes. Ces

observations restent des pistes de lecture, pas des vérités

absolues. Elles permettent surtout de sortir d’une idée reçue

tenace : celle qui associe systématiquement le sommeil partagé avec

un animal à une forme de dépendance affective ou d’anxiété. La

réalité, comme souvent en psychologie, est plus nuancée.

Un besoin de proximité

qui peut refléter un attachement sécurisant

Dans les années 1970, le psychologue John Bowlby développe la

théorie de l’attachement : les enfants nouent des liens avec

leurs figures de référence pour se sentir en sécurité. Ce mécanisme

ne s’arrête pas à l’enfance. Il se retrouve aussi dans

les liens tissés avec les animaux de compagnie. Le

coach de vie Sidhharrth S. Kumaar, cité par YourTango,

explique que laisser un animal partager son espace de sommeil

traduit une certaine aisance avec la présence émotionnelle, la

connexion et la confiance.

Cette envie de proximité physique peut s’inscrire dans une

relation d’attachement sécurisante, mais elle ne

permet pas, à elle seule, de déterminer le style d’attachement

d’une personne : d’autres facteurs entrent en jeu. Ce besoin de

partager son sommeil n’est pas non plus réservé à un profil de

personnalité précis, extraverti ou introverti : il dépend surtout

de la qualité du lien noué avec l’animal en question.

Une sensibilité qui favorise l’empathie envers l’animal

Pour la thérapeute Gloria Brame, les personnes qui dorment avec

leur animal comprennent que l’amour et le réconfort ne sont pas réservés aux

humains. Elles considèrent souvent leur compagnon

comme un membre de la famille à part entière. Le conseiller

conjugal Larry Michel, dont le petit chien dort dans son lit depuis

toujours, y voit une preuve d’acceptation et de présence

réciproques.

Accepter qu’un animal occupe l’espace le plus confortable de la

maison, y compris le lit, suppose de savoir interpréter ses signaux

non verbaux et de respecter ses préférences plutôt que d’imposer

les siennes. Cette disposition peut parfois traduire une

sensibilité et une capacité

d’empathie plus développée.

Une vraie tolérance face aux petits désagréments pendant la

nuit

Qui a déjà partagé son lit avec un chat connaît les réveils en

pleine nuit ou au petit matin. Ces moments où l’animal,

naturellement déjà réveillé, déambule, joue ou miaule. Accepter ces

petits désagréments de la cohabitation nocturne peut traduire une

certaine tolérance aux habitudes de son

animal.

Cela ne suffit évidemment pas à définir le tempérament d’une

personne dans son ensemble : on peut très bien se montrer patiente

avec son chat la nuit et beaucoup moins dans d’autres situations du

quotidien. Cette tolérance reste néanmoins révélatrice d’une chose

: la place que l’animal occupe dans l’équilibre

affectif de son propriétaire, au point d’accepter certains

sacrifices sur la qualité du repos.

Ce que la science dit vraiment de la qualité du sommeil

partagé

Une étude de la Mayo Clinic menée

en 2015 auprès de 150 patients d’un centre du sommeil a interrogé

les habitudes de 74 propriétaires d’animaux : 41 %

jugeaient la présence de leur animal neutre, voire bénéfique pour

leur sommeil, tandis que 20 % la trouvaient perturbatrice.

Une seconde étude de la même équipe, publiée en 2017, a mesuré

objectivement le sommeil de 40 personnes dormant avec leur chien :

l’efficacité du sommeil restait bonne lorsque l’animal dormait dans

la chambre, mais diminuait légèrement lorsqu’il dormait directement

sur le lit.

Plus récemment, une étude publiée en 2024 dans la revue Scientific Reports, portant sur 1591 adultes

américains dont 758 dormant avec leur animal, a observé une

qualité de sommeil plus faible et des symptômes

d’insomnie plus marqués chez les personnes qui

dorment avec leur animal, sans preuve que cette pratique protège

des effets du stress sur le sommeil. Les auteurs précisent que ces

résultats, de nature exploratoire, semblaient davantage concerner

les propriétaires de chiens que ceux de chats. Le lien affectif et

la qualité du repos restent donc deux choses bien distinctes, et

l’un ne garantit pas l’autre.

Ce qui compte, en définitive, c’est de vérifier si cette

organisation du sommeil vous convient, à vous comme à votre animal,

plutôt que de la juger à l’aune d’un supposé trait de

caractère.

DALLAS, Sept. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Apex Dental Partners, a dental partnership organization supporting dentists and affiliated practices, has been named No. 3,850 on the Inc. 5000 list of America's fastest-growing private companies, marking its eighth consecutive year on the list. The company achieved 67% revenue growth over the past three years, reflecting its continued investment in the doctors, teams, and practices it supports.
Published annually by Inc. magazine, the Inc. 5000 ranks privately held U.S. companies by percentage revenue growth over a three-year period. Apex's eight consecutive appearances reflect steady expansion while preserving its commitment to relationship-based dentistry.
Apex's approach to growth centers on supporting doctor partners personally and professionally through a community of colleagues, coaching, tools, technology, and education. "This recognition belongs to our doctor partners and their teams," said Matt Hale, President of Apex Dental Partners. "The growth we're celebrating this year is the direct result of their hard work, leadership, and commitment to their patients and communities."
That same long-term perspective guides Apex's plans for continued growth. "As we look ahead, our focus stays on building long-term partnerships, investing in our doctors, and staying true to the values of private practice," said David Lohmann, CEO of Apex. "That's the foundation we'll keep growing from."
About Apex Dental Partners
Apex Dental Partners is a dental partnership reimagining private practice dentistry for the next generation of clinicians committed to long-term, relationship-based, high-quality patient care. Through its non-branded Private Practice Reimagined® model, Apex combines the values of traditional dentistry with the resources and support of a larger organization. For more information, visit www.ApexDP.com

item.content:encoded:
TBC has been named the Best Corporate Bank by Euromoney for the third time, becoming the only bank from Georgia to receive the prestigious award in this category on three occasions.
The recognition from the international financial publication further underscores TBC’s leading position in Georgia’s corporate banking market, where the bank holds a 43% share of corporate lending.
Euromoney recognized TBC for its strong performance, innovation, digital transformation, and customer-centric approach. By adopting advanced technologies, TBC is simplifying business processes for its corporate clients, providing faster and more seamless services, and supporting business continuity.
In 2025, TBC introduced artificial intelligence tools into its corporate banking operating model, including AI Analyst Copilot, which automated the preparation of credit documentation. Combined with process improvements, the use of AI contributed to an 11% year-on-year reduction in the time required to provide financing.
TBC also introduced an online foreign-currency trading module, enabling customers to agree on exchange rates and execute transactions in real time through internet and mobile banking. These enhancements have increased operational efficiency and further improved the customer experience.
The development of TBC’s Customer Relationship Management (CRM) system has also enabled the bank to create offers that are more closely tailored to the needs of individual businesses. As a result, 70% of business proposals have converted into new client relationships.
“We are proud that TBC has won the Euromoney award for Best Corporate Bank every time we have been nominated in this category. This is further recognition of our leading position in the corporate banking market. TBC ranks first in corporate deposits, lending, and trade finance. We serve more than 6,700 corporate customers, which means that some of the largest businesses in Georgia place their trust in TBC. The Euromoney award reflects the daily work of our team, our focus on innovation, and the long-term partnerships we build with our customers. By providing solutions tailored to businesses’ needs and creating an outstanding customer experience, we will continue to partner with the private sector and contribute to the development of Georgia’s economy,” said Meri Chachanidze, Director of Corporate Banking Business Management at TBC.

item.content:encoded:
Seattle is putting polyamory in the spotlight after moving a step closer to protecting people in consensual relationships involving multiple partners from discrimination.
RELATED: Chris Gallant’s Past Isn’t a Problem. The Kink Shaming Is.
The Seattle City Council’s Housing, Arts and Civil Rights Committee unanimously voted to send a proposal to the full council that would expand the city’s civil rights code. Among other changes, the proposal would recognize “consensual relationships with multiple partners as an element of attitudes, preferences, and practices pertaining to sexual orientation.”
That may sound straightforward, but it also raises a question that tends to cause plenty of confusion: what exactly is the difference between polyamory and polygamy?
The terms are often used interchangeably, even though they describe different concepts. Seattle’s proposal is specifically concerned with consensual relationships involving multiple partners, rather than creating a system of multiple marriages.
RELATED: James Talarico’s Trans Sports Shift: What Changed?
What does polyamory mean here?
In the context of Seattle’s proposal, polyamory refers to consensual relationships involving multiple partners.
The emphasis is on consent. The proposal specifically refers to “consensual relationships with multiple partners,” meaning the relationships covered are ones in which the people involved are aware of and agree to the arrangement.
That distinction is important because the legislation is about protecting people from discrimination based on their family and relationship structure.
Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck, the bill’s sponsor, said the ordinance aims to “prohibit discrimination based on family and relationship structure as fully as possible.”
“We all know that every family is different, and we need to be clear that every family receives equal protection under the law,” Rinck said. “And chosen family is family.”
“This update reflects how people actually live,” Rinck added.
So where does polygamy fit in?
Polygamy and polyamory aren’t simply two words for exactly the same thing.
Polygamy is generally associated with marriage involving multiple spouses, while the Seattle proposal is addressing consensual relationships involving multiple partners and discrimination based on relationship or family structure.
That means the Seattle measure should not be described as an attempt to legalize multiple-spouse marriage. Instead, the proposal would add protections for people whose relationships and families fall outside more traditional structures.
And that distinction matters when discussing the legislation, because the issue before Seattle’s council is civil rights protection, not a change to the city’s marriage system.
Why are these protections being proposed?
The proposed protections would apply to areas including employment, housing, business licensure, places of public accommodation, park usage and “bias-free policing.” Under the proposal, people who experience unfair treatment could file complaints and seek a remedy through Seattle’s Office for Civil Rights.
Tyson Holman, co-chair of the Seattle Coalition for Family & Relationship Equity, testified in support of the proposal. Holman told council members that “being out” as poly can expose partners to discrimination, causing some people to “pretend to not love.”
“That’s why these protections are so important,” Holman said. “We don’t have to worry about losing our homes or our jobs or our families.”
Seattle’s Human Rights Commission had previously urged the mayor and City Council to consider the legislation, describing it as a “necessary and timely” evolution of the city’s approach to inclusivity. The commission said the legal framework “was largely built at a time when only a narrow definition of family and relationship was recognized.”
“As a result, many Seattle residents remain vulnerable to real and material harm,” the commission said.
The commission also pointed to multi-parent and multi-partner families, multi-generational households, chosen families, single parents, intentionally single individuals, and people in consensually nonmonogamous, asexual or aromantic relationships as groups that can face discrimination because their family structures fall outside traditional norms.
Seattle isn’t the first US city to recognize polyamory
Seattle would follow several other American cities that have adopted similar protections.
Somerville, Massachusetts, was the first U.S. city to formally recognize polyamorous relationships when it expanded its domestic partnership rules in 2020. The change extended certain benefits to poly partners, including hospital visitation rights and access to health insurance benefits.
In 2023, Somerville expanded its protections to specifically address discrimination in employment and interactions with police.
Portland, West Hollywood, Berkeley, Cambridge, Oakland, Olympia, Astoria and Hazel Park have also instituted similar protections, according to the report.
So while polygamy vs. polyamory can sound like a debate over terminology, Seattle’s proposal makes the practical distinction pretty clear: the city is considering protections for people in consensual multi-partner relationships and families, with the focus on preventing discrimination based on how those relationships are structured.
For anyone still mixing up the terms, that’s the key point to remember: polyamory and polygamy may both involve multiple partners, but Seattle’s proposed civil rights protections are specifically aimed at consensual relationship structures, not multiple-spouse marriage.
Source: Axios and NonMonogamyHelp
